Rental SQLCREATE TABLE Rental ( rental_id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT, customer_id INT NOT NULL, vehicle_id INT NOT NULL, pickup_branch_id INT NOT NULL, return_branch_id INT, pickup_date DATETIME NOT NULL, expected_return_date DATETIME NOT NULL, actual_return_date DATETIME, status VARCHAR(20) DEFAULT 'ACTIVE', total_amount DECIMAL(10,2), FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES Customer(customer_id), FOREIGN KEY (vehicle_id) REFERENCES Vehicle(vehicle_id), FOREIGN KEY (pickup_branch_id) REFERENCES Branch(branch_id), FOREIGN KEY (return_branch_id) REFERENCES Branch(branch_id), CHECK (expected_return_date > pickup_date), CHECK (total_amount >= 0) ); Payment SQLCREATE TABLE Payment ( payment_id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT, rental_id INT NOT NULL, amount DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL, payment_date DATETIME DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, payment_method VARCHAR(30), payment_status VARCHAR(20), FOREIGN KEY (rental_id) REFERENCES Rental(rental_id), CHECK (amount > 0) ); Maintenance SQLCREATE TABLE Maintenance ( maintenance_id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT, vehicle_id INT NOT NULL, maintenance_date DATE NOT NULL, description VARCHAR(255), cost DECIMAL(10,2), status VARCHAR(30), FOREIGN KEY (vehicle_id) REFERENCES Vehicle(vehicle_id), CHECK (cost >= 0) ); Important design decision A particularly important distinction is: VehicleCategory │ │ 1:N ▼ Vehicle │ │ 1:N ▼ Rental For example: VehicleCategory SUV ₹3000/day ↓ Vehicle KA01AB1234 Toyota Fortuner ↓ Rental #501 Customer: Rahul 10 Sept → 13 Sept You shouldn't store customer_id directly in Vehicle, because the same vehicle is rented by different customers at different times. Similarly, Reservation and Rental are separate: Reservation = customer intends to rent a vehicle/category. Rental = actual rental transaction after the vehicle is assigned/picked up. Key idea: The central transaction is Rental, while Vehicle, Customer, Branch, and VehicleCategory provide the entities around it. This structure also supports vehicle history, multiple branches, payments, reservations, and maintenance without duplicating data.

prompt: Explain how media queries are used to build responsive designs across device sizes.
response: Media Queries in Responsive Web Design A media query is a CSS feature that allows you to apply different styles depending on the characteristics of the user's device or viewport. The basic idea is: Same HTML │ ┌─────────┴─────────┐ │ │ Large screen Small screen │ │ Desktop styles Mobile styles │ │ └─────────┬─────────┘ ▼ Responsive UI 1. Basic Syntax CSS@media (max-width: 768px) { body { background: lightgray; } .container { width: 100%; } } This means: Apply these styles when the viewport width is 768px or smaller. 2. Common Breakpoints A typical responsive design might use: CSS/* Mobile */ @media (max-width: 576px) { /* mobile styles */ } /* Tablet */ @media (min-width: 577px) and (max-width: 992px) { /* tablet styles */ } /* Desktop */ @media (min-width: 993px) { /* desktop styles */ } However, these aren't mandatory device sizes. Good responsive design chooses breakpoints based on when the layout actually needs to change, rather than targeting specific phones. 3. Example: Responsive Navigation Desktop: ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Logo Home Courses About Contact Login │ └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘ Mobile: ┌──────────────────────┐ │ Logo ☰ │ └──────────────────────┘ CSS: CSS.nav-links { display: flex; gap: 30px; } .menu-button { display: none; } @media (max-width: 768px) { .nav-links { display: none; } .menu-button { display: block; } } On a large screen, the navigation links appear. Below 768px, they disappear and the menu button appears. 4. Changing Layout Columns Suppose you have three course cards: Desktop ┌─────────┐ ┌─────────┐ ┌─────────┐ │ Course 1│ │ Course 2│ │ Course 3│ └─────────┘ └─────────┘ └─────────┘ CSS: CSS.courses { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr); gap: 20px; } On mobile: ┌───────────────┐ │ Course 1 │ └───────────────┘ ┌───────────────┐ │ Course 2 │ └───────────────┘ ┌───────────────┐ │ Course 3 │ └───────────────┘ CSS@media (max-width: 768px) { .courses { grid-template-columns: 1fr; } } 5. Changing Font Sizes You can also adapt typography. CSSh1 { font-size: 48px; } @media (max-width: 768px) { h1 { font-size: 32px; } } So: Desktop → 48px Tablet → 32px Mobile → 32px This prevents large headings from taking up too much space on smaller screens. 6. Multiple Conditions Media queries can test multiple conditions. CSS@media (min-width: 600px) and (max-width: 1000px) { .sidebar { width: 200px; } } The styles apply only when: 600px ≤ viewport width ≤ 1000px You can also detect orientation: CSS@media (orientation: landscape) { .container { max-width: 1000px; } } 7. Mobile-First Design A very common modern approach is mobile-first CSS. Instead of starting with desktop: CSS/* Desktop first */ .card { width: 33%; } Start with the smallest layout: CSS.card { width: 100%; } Then progressively enhance it: CSS@media (min-width: 768px) { .card { width: 50%; } } @media (min-width: 1024px) { .card { width: 33.33%; } } Conceptually: Mobile │ ▼ 1 column │ ≥ 768px │ ▼ 2 columns │ ≥ 1024px │ ▼ 3 columns This approach is often easier to maintain because you start with the simplest layout and progressively add complexity. 8. Responsive Images Media queries can also modify images: CSS.hero-image { width: 600px; } @media (max-width: 768px) { .hero-image { width: 100%; } } But for many images, it's better to combine this with flexible sizing: CSSimg { max-width: 100%; height: auto; } This allows the image to shrink with its container. 9. Media Queries Are Only One Part of Responsiveness A common misconception is: Responsive design = media queries. Actually, responsive design usually combines: Responsive Design │ ├── Flexible layouts │ ├── Flexbox │ └── CSS Grid │ ├── Flexible dimensions │ ├── % │ ├── rem │ ├── vw/vh │ └── min/max functions │ ├── Responsive images │ └── Media queries ├── layout changes ├── typography ├── navigation └── spacing For example, instead of: CSS.container { width: 1200px; } prefer: CSS.container { width: 90%; max-width: 1200px; margin: auto; } Then use a media query only when the layout behavior needs to change. Key idea A media query essentially says: "If the screen/environment matches this condition, use these CSS rules." For example: CSS@media (max-width: 768px) { .sidebar { display: none; } .content { width: 100%; } } You're not creating a separate mobile website. You're creating one layout that adapts its presentation according to the available space.

prompt: Explain the differences between using Vite and Create React App for setting up a React project.
response:
Vite vs Create React App Both Vite and Create React App (CRA) were/are tools for setting up React projects, but they take different approaches to the development tooling. React's documentation explicitly says not to use Create React App for new applications. React 2. Development server This is one of the biggest practical differences. CRA The traditional CRA setup used Webpack to bundle the application during development. Conceptually: Your source code ↓ Webpack ↓ Development bundle ↓ Browser Vite Vite takes a more modern approach: Your source code ↓ Vite Dev Server ↓ Browser loads ES modules ↓ Only changed modules updated This is one reason Vite generally feels much faster when starting a development server and making changes. Vite's HMR system is designed to update modules without rebuilding the entire application. vitejs 3. Hot Module Replacement Suppose you have: JavaScriptfunction App() { return

Hello

Hello World

You could customize it, but doing so traditionally involved mechanisms such as: Bashnpm run eject After ejecting, you exposed a large amount of configuration. Important distinction: Vite isn't a React framework This is something beginners often misunderstand. Vite is primarily a build tool/development server. React 7. What should you use today? For a new React project, don't start with: Bashnpx create-react-app CRA is deprecated for new applications. React If you specifically want to learn React and build a client-side application yourself: Bashnpm create vite@latest is the modern build-tool route. Suggested project structure For a React-based SPA: src/ │ ├── app/ │ ├── App.jsx │ ├── router.jsx │ └── providers.jsx │ ├── components/ │ ├── Navbar/ │ ├── Sidebar/ │ ├── Button/ │ ├── Modal/ │ └── Loading/ │ ├── layouts/ │ ├── MainLayout.jsx │ └── AuthLayout.jsx │ ├── pages/ │ ├── Dashboard/ │ │ └── Dashboard.jsx │ │ │ ├── Products/ │ │ └── Products.jsx │ │ │ ├── Orders/ │ │ └── Orders.jsx │ │ │ ├── Profile/ │ │ └── Profile.jsx │ │ │ ├── Login/ │ │ └── Login.jsx │ │ │ └── NotFound/ │ └── NotFound.jsx │ ├── services/ │ ├── api.js │ ├── authService.js │ └── productService.js │ ├── hooks/ │ ├── useAuth.js │ └── useProducts.js │ ├── store/ │ ├── authStore.js │ └── cartStore.js │ ├── utils/ │ ├── validation.js │ └── formatters.js │ ├── styles/ │ └── global.css │ └── main.jsx 2. Routing layer The router determines which view should be displayed without reloading the entire page. For example: / → Dashboard /products → Products /products/:id → Product Details /orders → Orders /profile → Profile /login → Login Using React Router: JavaScriptconst router = createBrowserRouter([ { path: "/", element: , children: [ { path: "/", element: }, { path: "/products", element: }, { path: "/orders", element: }, { path: "/profile", element: } ] }, { path: "/login", element: } ]); The important SPA behavior is: Click link ↓ Router intercepts navigation ↓ URL changes ↓ Required view renders ↓ No full browser reload 3. Layout layer Instead of putting the navbar and sidebar into every page: Dashboard Navbar Sidebar Products Navbar Sidebar Orders Navbar Sidebar create a shared layout: MainLayout │ ├── Navbar │ ├── Sidebar │ └── Page Content │ ├── Dashboard ├── Products ├── Orders └── Profile Example: JavaScriptfunction MainLayout() { return ( <>
); } Outlet represents the currently selected route. 4. Component layer Components should be reusable. For example: components/ │ ├── Button ├── Modal ├── Table ├── Card ├── Navbar └── Sidebar A product page can then compose them: JavaScript The principle is: Pages compose components; components shouldn't know about entire pages. 5. State management Not every piece of state needs a global store. Separate state into categories: State │ ├── Local UI state │ └── modal open/closed │ ├── URL state │ └── search / filters / page number │ ├── Server state │ └── products / orders / users │ └── Global client state └── authentication / cart / theme For example: JavaScriptconst [isModalOpen, setIsModalOpen] = useState(false); can remain inside a component. Authentication might be managed globally: Auth Store ├── user ├── token/session └── authentication status For server data, a library such as TanStack Query can be useful because fetching, caching, refetching, and loading/error states are different from ordinary UI state. 6. API/service layer Avoid scattering API calls throughout components. Instead of: JavaScriptfunction Products() { fetch("https://api.example.com/products"); ... } create a service: JavaScriptexport async function getProducts() { const response = await fetch("/api/products"); if (!response.ok) { throw new Error("Failed to fetch products"); } return response.json(); } Then: JavaScriptfunction Products() { // Use getProducts() through // your data-fetching layer. } Architecture: Page │ ▼ Hook / Query │ ▼ Service │ ▼ API │ ▼ Backend This makes changing the backend API much easier. 7. prompt: Explain how to structure a scalable frontend architecture for a growing web application.
response: For a growing web application, the goal is not to create the most complicated folder structure. The goal is to make sure that adding a new feature does not require changing unrelated parts of the application. A scalable frontend architecture should separate features, UI, data fetching, state, routing, and infrastructure. 1. Start with feature-based architecture Instead of organizing everything by file type: components/ hooks/ services/ pages/ utils/ a larger application can become difficult to navigate because files belonging to one feature are scattered everywhere. Prefer a feature-oriented structure: src/ │ ├── app/ │ ├── router/ │ ├── providers/ │ └── App.jsx │ ├── features/ │ │ │ ├── authentication/ │ │ ├── components/ │ │ ├── hooks/ │ │ ├── services/ │ │ ├── store/ │ │ └── types/ │ │ │ ├── products/ │ │ ├── components/ │ │ ├── hooks/ │ │ ├── services/ │ │ ├── store/ │ │ └── types/ │ │ │ ├── orders/ │ │ ├── components/ │ │ ├── hooks/ │ │ ├── services/ │ │ └── types/ │ │ │ └── payments/ │ ├── components/ │ ├── Button/ │ ├── Modal/ │ ├── Table/ │ └── Input/ │ ├── layouts/ │ ├── DashboardLayout/ │ └── AuthLayout/ │ ├── lib/ │ ├── api/ │ ├── logger/ │ └── analytics/ │ ├── utils/ │ ├── formatting/ │ └── validation/ │ ├── styles/ │ └── main.jsx The important distinction is: features/ Product-specific code components/ Application-wide reusable UI lib/ Infrastructure/integrations utils/ Generic helpers 2. Think in layers A scalable application can be viewed like this: ┌───────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ UI │ │ Pages / Components / Layouts │ ├───────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ Feature Logic │ │ Products / Orders / Auth / Payments │ ├───────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ Data / State Layer │ │ Server State / Client State / Cache │ ├───────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ Infrastructure │ │ API / Analytics / Storage / Logging │ ├───────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ Backend │ └───────────────────────────────────────────┘ Each layer should have a clear responsibility. 3. Separate server state from UI state This becomes extremely important as an application grows. UI state Things such as: Modal open? Selected tab? Dropdown open? Form input? can usually stay close to the component. JavaScriptconst [isOpen, setIsOpen] = useState(false); Server state Things such as: Products Orders User profile Notifications Analytics come from the backend and usually need: caching loading states refetching error handling synchronization A data-fetching library such as TanStack Query can be useful here. Think: Application State │ ┌───────┴───────┐ │ │ Client Server State State │ │ UI preferences API data Modal state Products Filters Orders Theme Users Don't put every piece of state into Redux/global state simply because the application is large. 4. Keep API communication separate Avoid this pattern everywhere: JavaScriptfunction ProductPage() { fetch("/api/products") .then(...) .then(...); // UI... } Instead: ProductPage ↓ useProducts() ↓ productService ↓ API client ↓ Backend For example: JavaScript// features/products/services/productService.js export async function getProducts() { const response = await api.get("/products"); return response.data; } Then the feature can use it through a hook/query. This gives you a single place to modify API behavior later. 5. Create a shared API client Instead of repeating configuration: JavaScriptfetch("https://api.example.com/...") throughout the project, create an API layer. lib/ └── api/ ├── client.js ├── interceptors.js └── errors.js For example: JavaScriptconst api = axios.create({ baseURL: import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL, timeout: 10000 }); Now features use: JavaScriptapi.get("/products"); api.post("/orders"); api.get("/users/me"); This also gives you a central place for authentication headers, error handling, logging, etc. 6. Build a reusable design system As the application grows, you'll notice the same UI patterns appearing repeatedly. Instead of: ProductButton OrderButton ProfileButton PaymentButton create: components/ ├── Button ├── Input ├── Select ├── Modal ├── Table ├── Card └── Dropdown Then: JavaScript<Button variant="primary"> Buy Now </Button> This creates visual consistency across the application. For larger organizations, this can eventually become a proper design system with: Design tokens ↓ Components ↓ Patterns ↓ Pages 7. Keep feature ownership clear Suppose you have: features/ ├── products/ ├── orders/ └── payments/ The products feature should primarily own product-specific logic. products/ ├── components/ │ ├── ProductCard.jsx │ └── ProductFilters.jsx ├── hooks/ │ └── useProducts.js ├── services/ │ └── productService.js └── types/ └── product.js Then: ProductCard ↓ useProducts ↓ productService ↓ API This makes the feature relatively self-contained. 8. Don't create a giant global store A common mistake is: Redux Store │ ├── user ├── products ├── orders ├── modal ├── search ├── filters ├── forms ├── notifications ├── table sorting ├── dropdowns └── everything else This creates unnecessary coupling. Instead: Local state ↓ Component-specific state Feature state ↓ Feature-specific state Global state ↓ Actually global concerns For example: Authentication → Global Theme → Global Shopping cart → Potentially global Product filter → Product feature Modal → Local Form input → Local 9. Routing should reflect application structure For example: / ├── dashboard ├── products │ ├── /products │ ├── /products/:id │ └── /products/create ├── orders │ ├── /orders │ └── /orders/:id └── settings Your route structure should make the application hierarchy obvious. Protected areas can use layouts/route guards: Public ├── Login ├── Register └── Forgot Password Authenticated ├── Dashboard ├── Products ├── Orders └── Settings 10. Lazy-load large features You don't necessarily want the browser downloading every feature when the user first opens the application. Instead: Initial bundle │ ├── Dashboard ├── Navigation └── Core UI │ ▼ User opens Analytics │ ▼ Load Analytics code dynamically With React: JavaScriptconst Analytics = lazy(() => import("./features/analytics/Analytics")); This becomes increasingly useful as the application grows. 11. Establish dependency boundaries This is one of the more advanced architectural ideas. You don't want: Products ↓ Orders ↓ Payments ↓ Products ↓ Orders creating circular dependencies. Prefer controlled dependencies: Shared UI / | \ ↓ ↓ ↓ Products Orders Auth │ │ ▼ ▼ Services / API For example, a generic Button shouldn't import something from features/orders. A low-level component shouldn't depend on a high-level feature. 12. Add testing at different levels A scalable frontend needs more than manual testing. Testing │ ├── Unit tests │ └── utility functions │ ├── Component tests │ └── ProductCard │ ├── Integration tests │ └── Product → Cart flow │ └── E2E tests └── Login → Purchase → Payment You don't need hundreds of tests from day one. Build the testing strategy as the application grows. 13. Add observability Large applications eventually need to answer: "Why did this user's page fail?" Add: Frontend │ ├── Error tracking ├── Performance monitoring ├── Analytics ├── Logging └── User/session diagnostics For example: User ↓ React Application ↓ Error occurs ↓ Error tracking ↓ Stack trace + browser + route + release ↓ Developer This becomes extremely valuable in production. 14. Use TypeScript as the application grows For a small prototype: JavaScriptconst product = { name: "Laptop", price: 50000 }; In a larger application: TypeScriptinterface Product { id: string; name: string; price: number; category: string; } Now API responses, components, hooks, and services can share the same contracts. Backend API │ ▼ Product type │ ┌───┼────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ API Hook Component State This catches many integration errors before runtime. 15. A mature architecture Eventually, a large application might look like: src/ │ ├── app/ │ ├── router/ │ ├── providers/ │ ├── layouts/ │ └── config/ │ ├── features/ │ ├── auth/ │ ├── users/ │ ├── products/ │ ├── orders/ │ ├── payments/ │ └── analytics/ │ ├── components/ │ ├── ui/ │ ├── forms/ │ └── feedback/ │ ├── lib/ │ ├── api/ │ ├── auth/ │ ├── analytics/ │ └── monitoring/ │ ├── hooks/ │ ├── utils/ │ ├── types/ │ └── styles/ And the dependency direction should generally look like: ┌──────────────┐ │ App │ └──────┬───────┘ │ ┌─────────▼─────────┐ │ Features │ └─────────┬─────────┘ │ ┌───────────┼───────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ UI Hooks Services │ │ │ └───────────┼───────────┘ ▼ Infrastructure │ ▼ Backend The most important principle Don't optimize for a huge folder structure. Optimize for low coupling and clear ownership. A small application might begin as: components/ pages/ services/ and that's perfectly fine. As features grow, evolve toward: features/ auth/ products/ orders/ payments/ while keeping shared UI and infrastructure separate. The architecture should grow with the application, rather than forcing a complex enterprise structure onto a 5-page project from day one.

response: Here is a complete FastAPI REST API for a to-do list with Create, Read, Update, and Delete (CRUD) operations. It uses an in-memory list for simplicity, so data will reset when the server restarts. ========================================== # In-memory database # ========================================== todos: list[Todo] = [] next_id = 1 # ========================================== # CREATE # POST /todos # ========================================== @app.post("/todos", response_model=Todo, status_code=201) def create_todo(todo_data: TodoCreate): global next_id todo = Todo( id=next_id, title=todo_data.title, description=todo_data.description, completed=todo_data.completed ) todos.append(todo) next_id += 1 return todo # ========================================== # READ ALL # GET /todos # ========================================== @app.get("/todos", response_model=list[Todo]) def get_todos(): return todos # ========================================== # READ ONE # GET /todos/{todo_id} # ========================================== @app.get("/todos/{todo_id}", response_model=Todo) def get_todo(todo_id: int): for todo in todos: if todo.id == todo_id: return todo raise HTTPException( status_code=404, detail="Todo not found" ) # ========================================== # UPDATE # PUT /todos/{todo_id} # ========================================== @app.put("/todos/{todo_id}", response_model=Todo) def update_todo( todo_id: int, todo_data: TodoCreate ): for index, todo in enumerate(todos): if todo.id == todo_id: updated_todo = Todo( id=todo_id, title=todo_data.title, description=todo_data.description, completed=todo_data.completed ) todos[index] = updated_todo return updated_todo raise HTTPException( status_code=404, detail="Todo not found" ) # prompt: Write a Node.js Express server that handles user authentication with JWT tokens.
response: Below is a simple Node.js + Express authentication server using JWT. It demonstrates registration, login, password hashing with bcrypt, JWT creation, and a protected route. For learning, this uses an in-memory user store. In production, store users in a database and keep the JWT secret in an environment variable. Project structureauth-server/ │ ├── server.js ├── .env ├── package.json └── .gitignore1. Install dependenciesnpm init -y npm install express jsonwebtoken bcryptjs dotenv2. .envPORT=3000 JWT_SECRET=replace_this_with_a_long_random_secretNever commit .env to Git..gitignorenode_modules/ .env3. server.jsconst express = require("express"); const jwt = require("jsonwebtoken"); const bcrypt = require("bcryptjs"); require("dotenv").config(); const app = express(); app.use(express.json()); const PORT = process.env.PORT || 3000; const JWT_SECRET = process.env.JWT_SECRET; // ====================================== // Temporary in-memory user database // ====================================== const users = []; // ====================================== // Generate JWT // ====================================== function generateToken(user) { return jwt.sign( { userId: user.id, email: user.email }, JWT_SECRET, { expiresIn: "1h" } ); } // ====================================== // Authentication Middleware // ====================================== function authenticateToken(req, res, next) { const authHeader = req.headers.authorization; /* Expected format: Authorization: Bearer <token> */ if (!authHeader) { return res.status(401).json({ message: "Access token required" }); } const [scheme, token] = authHeader.split(" "); if (scheme !== "Bearer" || !token) { return res.status(401).json({ message: "Invalid authorization header" }); } try { const decoded = jwt.verify(token, JWT_SECRET); req.user = decoded; next(); } catch (error) { return res.status(403).json({ message: "Invalid or expired token" }); } } // ====================================== // Register // POST /api/auth/register // ====================================== app.post("/api/auth/register", async (req, res) => { try { const { email, password } = req.body; if (!email || !password) { return res.status(400).json({ message: "Email and password are required" }); } if (password.length < 8) { return res.status(400).json({ message: "Password must contain at least 8 characters" }); } const existingUser = users.find(user => user.email === email); if (existingUser) { return res.status(409).json({ message: "User already exists" }); } // Hash password const passwordHash = await bcrypt.hash(password, 12); const user = { id: users.length + 1, email, passwordHash }; users.push(user); res.status(201).json({ message: "User registered successfully" }); } catch (error) { res.status(500).json({ message: "Server error" }); } }); // ====================================== // Login // POST /api/auth/login // ====================================== app.post("/api/auth/login", async (req, res) => { try { const { email, password } = req.body; const user = users.find(user => user.email === email); /* Use the same generic error for both cases so the API doesn't reveal whether an email is registered. */ if (!user) { return res.status(401).json({ message: "Invalid email or password" }); } const passwordValid = await bcrypt.compare( password, user.passwordHash ); if (!passwordValid) { return res.status(401).json({ message: "Invalid email or password" }); } const token = generateToken(user); res.json({ message: "Login successful", token }); } catch (error) { res.status(500).json({ message: "Server error" }); } }); // ====================================== // Protected route // GET /api/profile // ====================================== app.get( "/api/profile", authenticateToken, (req, res) => { res.json({ message: "Authenticated successfully", user: req.user }); } ); // ====================================== // Start server // ====================================== app.listen(PORT, () => { console.log( `Server running on http://localhost:${PORT}` ); });4. Authentication flow REGISTER │ ▼ Email + Password │ ▼ bcrypt.hash() │ ▼ Store user │ ▼ Registration successful LOGIN │ ▼ Email + Password │ ▼ Find user in DB │ ▼ bcrypt.compare() │ ┌──────┴──────┐ NO YES │ │ ▼ ▼ 401 Generate JWT │ ▼ Return tokenThen the client uses the token for protected requests:Client │ │ Authorization: Bearer <JWT> ▼ Express │ ▼ authenticateToken() │ ├── Invalid ──► 401/403 │ └── Valid │ ▼ req.user │ ▼ Protected route5. Testing the APIRegisterPOST /api/auth/register Content-Type: application/json{ "email": "student@example.com", "password": "StrongPassword123" }LoginPOST /api/auth/login Content-Type: application/json{ "email": "student@example.com", "password": "StrongPassword123" }Response:{ "message": "Login successful", "token": "eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIs..." }Access protected routeSend the JWT in the Authorization header:GET /api/profile Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIs...Response:{ "message": "Authenticated successfully", "user": { "userId": 1, "email": "student@example.com", "iat": 1720000000, "exp": 1720003600 } }Important security pointsThe JWT should not contain sensitive information such as passwords. JWT payloads are encoded, not encrypted.For a production application, also use:Password ↓ bcrypt/Argon2 ↓ Password hash ↓ Database JWT ↓ Short expiration ↓ Secure transport (HTTPS)And consider:Store secrets in environment/secret management systems, not source code.Use HTTPS.Use short-lived access tokens.Implement refresh-token rotation if long-lived sessions are needed.Validate and rate-limit login attempts.Don't store plaintext passwords.Use secure, appropriately configured cookies when using cookie-based session/token storage.Add logout/revocation strategy appropriate to your token architecture.Store users in PostgreSQL/MySQL/MongoDB rather than the in-memory array.Key idea: JWT authentication has two separate responsibilities: login creates a signed token, while middleware verifies that token before allowing access to protected routes.Add a clear setup and run commandExplain the in-memory database limitationHandle missing or invalid JWT configuration

prompt: Explain how Pydantic is used for request validation in FastAPI applications.
response: Pydantic Request Validation in FastAPI Pydantic is the library FastAPI uses to define and validate the structure of incoming data. Instead of manually checking every field: Pythonif not name: ... if not isinstance(age, int): ... you define the expected structure once using a Pydantic model, and FastAPI validates incoming requests against it. 1. Basic Example Pythonfrom fastapi import FastAPI from pydantic import BaseModel app = FastAPI() class Student(BaseModel): name: str age: int email: str @app.post("/students") def create_student(student: Student): return { "message": "Student created", "student": student } Now the API expects JSON like: JSON{ "name": "Rahul", "age": 20, "email": "rahul@example.com" } FastAPI receives the request and essentially performs: HTTP Request │ ▼ FastAPI │ ▼ Pydantic Model │ ├── Valid ───────► Route function │ └── Invalid │ ▼ 422 Validation Error 2. Type Validation Consider: Pythonclass Student(BaseModel): name: str age: int A valid request: JSON{ "name": "Rahul", "age": 20 } An invalid request: JSON{ "name": "Rahul", "age": "twenty" } Pydantic detects that "twenty" cannot be interpreted as the required integer and FastAPI returns a validation error. 3. Required vs Optional Fields Fields without defaults are required: Pythonclass Student(BaseModel): name: str age: int Both must be provided. You can give a default: Pythonclass Student(BaseModel): name: str age: int = 18 Now age is optional from the client's perspective: JSON{ "name": "Rahul" } will use: age = 18 For nullable/optional fields in modern Pydantic, you can explicitly use: Pythonfrom typing import Optional class Student(BaseModel): name: str age: int phone: Optional[str] = None 4. Constraints Pydantic can validate more than just data types. For example: Pythonfrom pydantic import BaseModel, Field class Student(BaseModel): name: str = Field( min_length=3, max_length=50 ) age: int = Field( ge=17, le=100 ) Now: name 3 ─────────────── 50 characters age 17 ────────────── 100 A request such as: JSON{ "name": "A", "age": 12 } will fail validation. 5. Email Validation Pydantic can also validate specialized types. Pythonfrom pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr class Student(BaseModel): name: str email: EmailStr age: int Now: JSON{ "name": "Rahul", "email": "rahul@example.com", "age": 20 } is valid. But: JSON{ "name": "Rahul", "email": "hello", "age": 20 } fails email validation. You may need the email extra dependency depending on your environment: Bashpip install "pydantic[email]" 6. Nested Models Pydantic becomes particularly useful when requests have complex structures. Pythonfrom pydantic import BaseModel class Address(BaseModel): city: str state: str pincode: str class Student(BaseModel): name: str age: int address: Address The request can be: JSON{ "name": "Rahul", "age": 20, "address": { "city": "Hyderabad", "state": "Telangana", "pincode": "500001" } } FastAPI validates the entire nested structure. Student │ ├── name → str ├── age → int └── address → Address │ ├── city → str ├── state → str └── pincode → str 7. Lists You can validate lists too. Pythonfrom pydantic import BaseModel class Course(BaseModel): name: str credits: int class Student(BaseModel): name: str courses: list[Course] Request: JSON{ "name": "Rahul", "courses": [ { "name": "DBMS", "credits": 4 }, { "name": "Operating Systems", "credits": 3 } ] } Pydantic validates each course. 8. Custom Validation You can create your own validation rules using Pydantic validators. For example, suppose a username must not contain spaces. Pythonfrom pydantic import BaseModel, field_validator class User(BaseModel): username: str @field_validator("username") @classmethod def validate_username(cls, value): if " " in value: raise ValueError( "Username cannot contain spaces" ) return value Now: "rahul123" → Valid "rahul kumar" → Invalid 9. Validation Error Returned by FastAPI Suppose your model is: Pythonclass Student(BaseModel): name: str age: int and the client sends: JSON{ "name": "Rahul", "age": "abc" } FastAPI automatically generates a structured validation response similar to: JSON{ "detail": [ { "type": "int_parsing", "loc": ["body", "age"], "msg": "Input should be a valid integer" } ] } You don't have to manually create this error response. 10. Request Validation vs Response Validation Pydantic isn't only useful for incoming requests. You can also define what your API returns. Pythonclass StudentResponse(BaseModel): id: int name: str age: int @app.get( "/students/{student_id}", response_model=StudentResponse ) def get_student(student_id: int): return { "id": student_id, "name": "Rahul", "age": 20 } Now you have: Client │ │ JSON Request ▼ Pydantic │ │ validated data ▼ FastAPI Route │ │ application logic ▼ Pydantic Response Model │ ▼ JSON Response This gives you a contract on both sides. 11. Why This Is Better Than Manual Validation Without Pydantic: Python@app.post("/students") def create_student(data): if "name" not in data: ... if not isinstance(data["age"], int): ... if data["age"] < 17: ... if "email" not in data: ... ... This quickly becomes messy. With Pydantic: Pythonclass Student(BaseModel): name: str age: int = Field(ge=17) email: EmailStr Then: Python@app.post("/students") def create_student(student: Student): ... The route becomes much cleaner. Complete example Pythonfrom fastapi import FastAPI from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr, Field app = FastAPI() class Student(BaseModel): name: str = Field( min_length=3, max_length=50 ) age: int = Field( ge=17, le=100 ) email: EmailStr @app.post("/students") def create_student(student: Student): return { "message": "Student accepted", "data": student } A request: JSON{ "name": "Rahul", "age": 20, "email": "rahul@example.com" } passes through: JSON Request │ ▼ ┌──────────────────┐ │ Pydantic Model │ ├──────────────────┤ │ name → str │ │ age → int │ │ age >= 17 │ │ age <= 100 │ │ email → EmailStr │ └────────┬─────────┘ │ ┌──────┴───────┐ │ │ Valid Invalid │ │ ▼ ▼ Route executes 422 Error Key idea Pydantic is the data contract between the client and your FastAPI application. You describe: What data should look like and Pydantic/FastAPI handles: Checking whether the incoming data actually satisfies that contract. This is one of the reasons FastAPI can provide automatic validation, structured error responses, and OpenAPI/Swagger documentation from the same Python type definitions.

prompt: Design REST API routing for an e-commerce backend covering products, orders, and users.
response: REST API Routing for an E-Commerce Backend A clean REST API should organize endpoints around resources rather than actions. The main resources are: Users Products Orders A practical architecture is: Client │ ▼ API Gateway / Backend │ ├── /api/v1/users ├── /api/v1/products └── /api/v1/orders │ ▼ Database 1. API Route Structure Use versioning from the beginning: /api/v1 │ ├── /users │ ├── GET /users │ ├── POST /users │ ├── GET /users/{userId} │ ├── PATCH /users/{userId} │ └── DELETE /users/{userId} │ ├── /products │ ├── GET /products │ ├── POST /products │ ├── GET /products/{productId} │ ├── PATCH /products/{productId} │ └── DELETE /products/{productId} │ └── /orders ├── GET /orders ├── POST /orders ├── GET /orders/{orderId} ├── PATCH /orders/{orderId} └── DELETE /orders/{orderId} 2. User Routes Create user httpPOST /api/v1/users Request: JSON{ "name": "Rahul Kumar", "email": "rahul@example.com", "password": "********" } Response: JSON{ "id": 101, "name": "Rahul Kumar", "email": "rahul@example.com" } The password should never be returned. Get user httpGET /api/v1/users/101 Update user httpPATCH /api/v1/users/101 JSON{ "name": "Rahul Sharma" } Delete user httpDELETE /api/v1/users/101 3. Authentication Routes Authentication is usually separated from general user management: /api/v1/auth │ ├── POST /register ├── POST /login ├── POST /refresh └── POST /logout For example: httpPOST /api/v1/auth/login JSON{ "email": "rahul@example.com", "password": "********" } Response might contain an access token/session information. JSON{ "access_token": "...", "token_type": "Bearer" } 4. Product Routes Products are another major resource. /api/v1/products Get products httpGET /api/v1/products Possible query parameters: httpGET /api/v1/products?category=electronics&limit=20&page=2 Filtering: httpGET /api/v1/products?min_price=1000&max_price=50000 Searching: httpGET /api/v1/products?search=laptop Sorting: httpGET /api/v1/products?sort=price&order=asc These are query parameters because they modify how the collection is retrieved rather than identifying a different resource. Get a specific product httpGET /api/v1/products/501 Response: JSON{ "id": 501, "name": "Laptop", "price": 65000, "category": "Electronics", "stock": 20 } Create product httpPOST /api/v1/products Update product httpPATCH /api/v1/products/501 Delete product httpDELETE /api/v1/products/501 5. Category Routes Categories can be modeled as their own resource: /api/v1/categories │ ├── GET /categories ├── POST /categories ├── GET /categories/{categoryId} ├── PATCH /categories/{categoryId} └── DELETE /categories/{categoryId} You can then filter products: httpGET /api/v1/products?category_id=10 This is generally preferable to creating routes such as: /products/electronics /products/laptops /products/cheap-products for every possible filter. 6. Order Routes Orders represent a customer's purchase. /api/v1/orders Create order httpPOST /api/v1/orders Example: JSON{ "items": [ { "product_id": 501, "quantity": 2 }, { "product_id": 502, "quantity": 1 } ], "shipping_address_id": 20 } The backend should calculate the actual price from trusted product data rather than trusting a client-supplied total. Get orders httpGET /api/v1/orders For an authenticated user, this could return that user's orders. Admin functionality could support: httpGET /api/v1/orders?status=shipped Get specific order httpGET /api/v1/orders/9001 Update order httpPATCH /api/v1/orders/9001 For example, an authorized administrative operation could change status: JSON{ "status": "SHIPPED" } Delete/cancel Rather than blindly deleting historical orders, e-commerce systems commonly model cancellation: httpPOST /api/v1/orders/9001/cancel or: httpPATCH /api/v1/orders/9001 JSON{ "status": "CANCELLED" } The exact choice depends on the domain and state-transition rules. 7. User-Specific Orders There are two reasonable approaches. Query-based httpGET /api/v1/orders?user_id=101 Nested resource httpGET /api/v1/users/101/orders For an authenticated customer's own orders, an endpoint such as: httpGET /api/v1/me/orders is often convenient: /api/v1/me │ ├── GET /profile ├── PATCH /profile └── GET /orders The server determines the user from the authentication context rather than trusting a client-provided user ID. 8. Order Items An order contains multiple products: Order │ ├── OrderItem → Product ├── OrderItem → Product └── OrderItem → Product You could expose: httpGET /api/v1/orders/9001/items But you don't necessarily need a separate public endpoint if order retrieval already returns its items: JSON{ "id": 9001, "status": "CONFIRMED", "items": [ { "product_id": 501, "name": "Laptop", "quantity": 2, "unit_price": 65000 } ], "total": 130000 } 9. Recommended Complete API /api/v1 │ ├── auth │ ├── POST /register │ ├── POST /login │ ├── POST /refresh │ └── POST /logout │ ├── users │ ├── GET / │ ├── POST / │ ├── GET /{userId} │ ├── PATCH /{userId} │ └── DELETE /{userId} │ ├── me │ ├── GET /profile │ ├── PATCH /profile │ └── GET /orders │ ├── products │ ├── GET / │ ├── POST / │ ├── GET /{productId} │ ├── PATCH /{productId} │ └── DELETE /{productId} │ ├── categories │ ├── GET / │ ├── POST / │ ├── GET /{categoryId} │ ├── PATCH /{categoryId} │ └── DELETE /{categoryId} │ └── orders ├── GET / ├── POST / ├── GET /{orderId} ├── PATCH /{orderId} └── POST /{orderId}/cancel 10. Backend architecture The routes shouldn't contain all the business logic. Instead: HTTP Request │ ▼ ┌───────────────┐ │ Router │ │ /products/... │ └───────┬───────┘ │ ▼ ┌───────────────┐ │ Controller │ │ Parse request │ └───────┬───────┘ │ ▼ ┌───────────────┐ │ Service Layer │ │ Business logic│ └───────┬───────┘ │ ▼ ┌───────────────┐ │ Repository │ │ Database │ └───────┬───────┘ │ ▼ Database For example: POST /api/v1/orders │ ▼ Order Router │ ▼ Order Service │ ├── Validate products ├── Check inventory ├── Calculate prices ├── Create order └── Reserve/update stock │ ▼ Database This prevents controllers from becoming enormous. 11. HTTP methods and their meaning MethodTypical meaningExampleGETRetrieveGET /productsPOSTCreate/actionPOST /ordersPUTReplace a resourcePUT /users/101PATCHPartially updatePATCH /products/501DELETERemoveDELETE /products/501 A useful rule is: URLs identify resources; HTTP methods describe what you want to do with them. So prefer: httpGET /products/501 over: httpGET /getProduct/501 and: httpPOST /orders over: httpPOST /createOrder 12. Final architecture E-Commerce Frontend │ ▼ /api/v1 │ ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐ │ │ │ ▼ ▼ ▼ Auth Products Orders │ │ │ ▼ ▼ ▼ Auth Service Product Service Order Service │ │ │ └────────────────┼────────────────┘ ▼ Repository Layer │ ▼ Database Key design principle: keep the API resource-oriented, versioned, predictable, and stateless at the HTTP layer, while putting business rules in service layers rather than directly inside route handlers.

prompt: Write middleware in Express.js that logs incoming requests and handles errors.
response: In Express.js, middleware functions sit between the incoming request and the route handler. For this requirement, we can create two middleware functions: Request logger — logs method, URL, status code, and response time. Error handler — catches errors and returns a consistent JSON response. server.jsconst express = require("express"); const app = express(); app.use(express.json()); // ============================================ // 1. Request Logging Middleware // ============================================ function requestLogger(req, res, next) { const startTime = Date.now(); // Runs when the response is finished res.on("finish", () => { const duration = Date.now() - startTime; console.log( `${req.method} ${req.originalUrl} ` + `${res.statusCode} - ${duration}ms` ); }); next(); } app.use(requestLogger); // ============================================ // 2. Example Routes // ============================================ app.get("/", (req, res) => { res.json({ message: "Server is running" }); }); app.get("/users", (req, res) => { res.json({ users: [ { id: 1, name: "Rahul" }, { id: 2, name: "Priya" } ] }); }); // ============================================ // Example route that throws an error // ============================================ app.get("/error", (req, res, next) => { const error = new Error("Something went wrong"); next(error); }); // ============================================ // 3. 404 Handler // ============================================ app.use((req, res, next) => { const error = new Error( `Route not found: ${req.method} ${req.originalUrl}` ); error.statusCode = 404; next(error); }); // ============================================ // 4. Global Error-Handling Middleware // ============================================ app.use((err, req, res, next) => { console.error("ERROR:", err.stack); const statusCode = err.statusCode || 500; res.status(statusCode).json({ success: false, message: statusCode === 500 ? "Internal Server Error" : err.message }); }); // ============================================ // Start server // ============================================ const PORT = 3000; app.listen(PORT, () => { console.log( `Server running on http://localhost:${PORT}` ); });How the middleware worksThe request passes through the middleware in order:Client │ │ GET /users ▼ ┌─────────────────────┐ │ Request Logger │ │ │ │ start timer │ │ next() │ └──────────┬──────────┘ │ ▼ ┌─────────────────────┐ │ Route Handler │ │ │ │ GET /users │ └──────────┬──────────┘ │ ▼ JSON Response │ ▼ Logger's "finish" event │ ▼ GET /users 200 - 4msError flowIf a route calls:next(error);Express skips normal middleware and moves to the error-handling middleware:Route │ │ next(error) ▼ ┌─────────────────────┐ │ Error Middleware │ │ │ │ Log error │ │ Determine status │ │ Send JSON response │ └─────────────────────┘The important distinction is the four-argument signature:app.use((err, req, res, next) => { // error handling });Express recognizes this as error-handling middleware because it has:err → req → res → nextExample outputFor:GET /usersthe console might show:GET /users 200 - 3msFor:GET /does-not-existthe response would be:{ "success": false, "message": "Route not found: GET /does-not-exist" }For an unexpected server error:{ "success": false, "message": "Internal Server Error" }Key idea: request middleware runs before/around route processing, while error middleware provides a centralized place to catch, log, and format errors instead of duplicating error-handling code in every route.Add setup and test commandsExplain production-safe error responsesClarify asynchronous error handling

prompt: Explain async programming in Node.js using an example of concurrent API calls.
response: Async Programming in Node.js Node.js uses asynchronous, non-blocking I/O, which means it can start an operation such as an API request and continue doing other work instead of waiting for that request to finish. A very common example is making multiple API calls concurrently. 1. The problem with sequential API calls Suppose you need data from three APIs: API 1 → User API 2 → Orders API 3 → Recommendations A sequential approach does this: JavaScriptconst user = await fetch("/user"); const orders = await fetch("/orders"); const recommendations = await fetch("/recommendations"); The execution is: Start User API │ └────── 2 seconds ──────► Done │ ▼ Start Orders API │ 3 seconds │ ▼ Start Recommendations │ 1 second │ ▼ Done Total ≈ 6 seconds The problem isn't that Node.js is blocking the entire process. Your code is choosing to wait for each promise before starting the next request. 2. Concurrent API calls with Promise.all() If the requests are independent, start them together: JavaScriptconst [user, orders, recommendations] = await Promise.all([ fetch("/user"), fetch("/orders"), fetch("/recommendations") ]); Now: ┌──► User API ──────────► 2 sec ──┐ │ │ Start ───────┼──► Orders API ────────► 3 sec ──┼──► Continue │ │ └──► Recommendations ──► 1 sec ──┘ Total ≈ 3 seconds The total time is approximately the duration of the slowest request rather than the sum of all requests. 3. Complete Node.js example JavaScriptconst express = require("express"); const app = express(); // Simulated asynchronous API calls async function getUser() { return new Promise(resolve => { setTimeout(() => { resolve({ id: 101, name: "Rahul" }); }, 2000); }); } async function getOrders() { return new Promise(resolve => { setTimeout(() => { resolve([ { id: 1, product: "Laptop" }, { id: 2, product: "Mouse" } ]); }, 3000); }); } async function getRecommendations() { return new Promise(resolve => { setTimeout(() => { resolve([ "Keyboard", "Monitor" ]); }, 1000); }); } // Route app.get("/dashboard", async (req, res) => { try { const [ user, orders, recommendations ] = await Promise.all([ getUser(), getOrders(), getRecommendations() ]); res.json({ user, orders, recommendations }); } catch (error) { res.status(500).json({ message: "Failed to load dashboard" }); } }); app.listen(3000, () => { console.log("Server running on port 3000"); }); When /dashboard is requested, Node.js starts all three asynchronous operations without waiting for one to finish before starting the next. 4. What is actually happening? This is the important part. When Node.js reaches: JavaScriptgetOrders() it starts the asynchronous operation. Node.js doesn't sit there doing: WAIT WAIT WAIT Instead, the operation is handled by the underlying asynchronous I/O mechanisms. Conceptually: JavaScript │ ▼ Node.js │ ├──────────────► User API │ ├──────────────► Orders API │ └──────────────► Recommendations API When operations finish, their promises become fulfilled and the corresponding continuations can run. 5. Why await doesn't necessarily mean "everything stops" Consider: JavaScriptconst result = await fetch(url); await pauses that async function's execution until the promise settles. It does not mean: Stop the entire Node.js server. For example: JavaScriptapp.get("/data", async (req, res) => { const result = await fetch("https://example.com"); res.json(await result.json()); }); While this request is waiting for the network: Request A │ ├── waiting for API ──────────┐ │ │ │ Node.js can │ handle other work │ │ Request B ──────────────────────┘ Another incoming request can be processed. That's the essence of Node.js's non-blocking I/O model. 6. Promise.all() vs sequential await Sequential JavaScriptconst a = await apiA(); const b = await apiB(); const c = await apiC(); Timeline: A ──────────► B ───────────────► C ─────► Concurrent JavaScriptconst [a, b, c] = await Promise.all([ apiA(), apiB(), apiC() ]); Timeline: A ──────────► B ───────────────► C ─────► If: A = 2 sec B = 3 sec C = 1 sec approximately: Sequential ≈ 2 + 3 + 1 = 6 sec Concurrent ≈ max(2, 3, 1) = 3 sec 7. What happens if one request fails? With: JavaScriptawait Promise.all([ apiA(), apiB(), apiC() ]); if one promise rejects, Promise.all() rejects. A ─────────► Success B ────────► ERROR C ─────────────► Success │ ▼ Promise.all() │ ▼ catch For example: JavaScripttry { const [a, b, c] = await Promise.all([ apiA(), apiB(), apiC() ]); } catch (error) { console.error(error); } 8. When you don't want one failure to affect the others Use Promise.allSettled(): JavaScriptconst results = await Promise.allSettled([ apiA(), apiB(), apiC() ]); You might get: JavaScript[ { status: "fulfilled", value: ... }, { status: "rejected", reason: ... }, { status: "fulfilled", value: ... } ] This is useful for dashboards where you still want partial results. The mental model Think of Node.js asynchronous programming like this: Node.js │ ┌────────┼────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ API A API B API C │ │ │ ▼ ▼ ▼ Result Result Result └────────┼────────┘ ▼ Your code Don't confuse concurrency with parallelism. For network/API calls, Node.js can have many I/O operations in flight concurrently without requiring one JavaScript thread per request. Key idea If operations are independent, don't write: JavaScriptconst a = await A(); const b = await B(); const c = await C(); Prefer: JavaScriptconst [a, b, c] = await Promise.all([ A(), B(), C() ]); when you need all three results. This is one of the most important patterns for building fast Node.js API backends.

prompt: Build a Spring Boot REST controller for managing employee records.
response: Below is a simple Spring Boot REST API for managing employee records. It demonstrates the standard flow: HTTP Request ↓ EmployeeController ↓ EmployeeService ↓ EmployeeRepository ↓ Database It supports Create, Read, Update, and Delete (CRUD) operations. Project structuresrc/main/java/com/example/employees/ │ ├── EmployeeApplication.java │ ├── controller/ │ └── EmployeeController.java │ ├── model/ │ └── Employee.java │ ├── service/ │ └── EmployeeService.java │ └── repository/ └── EmployeeRepository.java1. Employee EntityEmployee.javapackage com.example.employees.model; import jakarta.persistence.*; @Entity @Table(name = "employees") public class Employee { @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY) private Long id; private String name; private String email; private String department; private double salary; public Employee() { } public Employee( String name, String email, String department, double salary ) { this.name = name; this.email = email; this.department = department; this.salary = salary; } // Getters and Setters public Long getId() { return id; } public void setId(Long id) { this.id = id; } public String getName() { return name; } public void setName(String name) { this.name = name; } public String getEmail() { return email; } public void setEmail(String email) { this.email = email; } public String getDepartment() { return department; } public void setDepartment(String department) { this.department = department; } public double getSalary() { return salary; } public void setSalary(double salary) { this.salary = salary; } }2. RepositoryEmployeeRepository.javapackage com.example.employees.repository; import com.example.employees.model.Employee; import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.JpaRepository; public interface EmployeeRepository extends JpaRepository<Employee, Long> { }JpaRepository automatically provides methods such as:save() findAll() findById() deleteById() existsById()So you don't have to manually write SQL for basic CRUD operations.3. Service LayerEmployeeService.javapackage com.example.employees.service; import com.example.employees.model.Employee; import com.example.employees.repository.EmployeeRepository; import org.springframework.stereotype.Service; import java.util.List; @Service public class EmployeeService { private final EmployeeRepository repository; public EmployeeService(EmployeeRepository repository) { this.repository = repository; } // Get all employees public List<Employee> getAllEmployees() { return repository.findAll(); } // Get employee by ID public Employee getEmployeeById(Long id) { return repository.findById(id) .orElseThrow(() -> new RuntimeException( "Employee not found: " + id ) ); } // Create employee public Employee createEmployee(Employee employee) { return repository.save(employee); } // Update employee public Employee updateEmployee( Long id, Employee updatedEmployee ) { Employee existingEmployee = getEmployeeById(id); existingEmployee.setName( updatedEmployee.getName() ); existingEmployee.setEmail( updatedEmployee.getEmail() ); existingEmployee.setDepartment( updatedEmployee.getDepartment() ); existingEmployee.setSalary( updatedEmployee.getSalary() ); return repository.save(existingEmployee); } // Delete employee public void deleteEmployee(Long id) { if (!repository.existsById(id)) { throw new RuntimeException( "Employee not found: " + id ); } repository.deleteById(id); } }4. REST ControllerEmployeeController.javapackage com.example.employees.controller; import com.example.employees.model.Employee; import com.example.employees.service.EmployeeService; import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus; import org.springframework.http.ResponseEntity; import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*; import java.util.List; @RestController @RequestMapping("/api/employees") public class EmployeeController { private final EmployeeService employeeService; public EmployeeController( EmployeeService employeeService ) { this.employeeService = employeeService; } // ========================================== // GET /api/employees // Get all employees // ========================================== @GetMapping public ResponseEntity<List<Employee>> getAllEmployees() { return ResponseEntity.ok( employeeService.getAllEmployees() ); } // ========================================== // GET /api/employees/{id} // Get employee by ID // ========================================== @GetMapping("/{id}") public ResponseEntity<Employee> getEmployeeById( @PathVariable Long id ) { return ResponseEntity.ok( employeeService.getEmployeeById(id) ); } // ========================================== // POST /api/employees // Create employee // ========================================== @PostMapping public ResponseEntity<Employee> createEmployee( @RequestBody Employee employee ) { Employee createdEmployee = employeeService.createEmployee(employee); return ResponseEntity .status(HttpStatus.CREATED) .body(createdEmployee); } // ========================================== // PUT /api/employees/{id} // Update employee // ========================================== @PutMapping("/{id}") public ResponseEntity<Employee> updateEmployee( @PathVariable Long id, @RequestBody Employee employee ) { Employee updatedEmployee = employeeService.updateEmployee( id, employee ); return ResponseEntity.ok(updatedEmployee); } // ========================================== // DELETE /api/employees/{id} // Delete employee // ========================================== @DeleteMapping("/{id}") public ResponseEntity<Void> deleteEmployee( @PathVariable Long id ) { employeeService.deleteEmployee(id); return ResponseEntity.noContent().build(); } }5. Main ApplicationEmployeeApplication.javapackage com.example.employees; import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication; import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication; @SpringBootApplication public class EmployeeApplication { public static void main(String[] args) { SpringApplication.run( EmployeeApplication.class, args ); } }6. API EndpointsMethodEndpointPurposeGET/api/employeesGet all employeesGET/api/employees/{id}Get one employeePOST/api/employeesCreate employeePUT/api/employees/{id}Update employeeDELETE/api/employees/{id}Delete employee7. Creating an EmployeeSend:POST /api/employees Content-Type: application/json{ "name": "Rahul Kumar", "email": "rahul@example.com", "department": "Engineering", "salary": 75000 }The controller receives the JSON through:@RequestBody Employee employeeSpring/Jackson converts the JSON into an Employee object.Then:JSON ↓ @RequestBody ↓ Employee object ↓ EmployeeController ↓ EmployeeService ↓ EmployeeRepository ↓ Database8. Getting an EmployeeGET /api/employees/5The:@PathVariable Long idextracts 5 from the URL./api/employees/5 ↑ id = 5The service then searches the database.9. Updating an EmployeePUT /api/employees/5 Content-Type: application/json{ "name": "Rahul Sharma", "email": "rahul@example.com", "department": "AI Engineering", "salary": 85000 }The controller receives both:@PathVariable Long idand:@RequestBody Employee employeeSo the request contains:URL │ └── employee ID = 5 Body │ ├── name ├── email ├── department └── salary10. Why use Controller → Service → Repository?Avoid putting all database/business logic directly inside the controller.Instead: HTTP │ ▼ ┌──────────────────┐ │ EmployeeController│ │ API layer │ └────────┬─────────┘ │ ▼ ┌──────────────────┐ │ EmployeeService │ │ Business logic │ └────────┬─────────┘ │ ▼ ┌──────────────────┐ │ EmployeeRepository│ │ Data access │ └────────┬─────────┘ │ ▼ DatabaseThe controller handles HTTP, the service handles business logic, and the repository handles persistence.For a production application, you would typically add DTOs, Bean Validation (@Valid, @NotBlank, @Email, etc.), a global @ControllerAdvice exception handler, pagination/filtering, and database-specific configuration rather than exposing the JPA entity directly through the API.

prompt: Design an API integration strategy for connecting a frontend app to a third-party payment gateway.
response: API Integration Strategy: Frontend + Third-Party Payment Gateway For a payment system, the frontend should not directly control or verify the payment. The backend should act as the trusted integration layer between your application and the payment gateway. A good architecture is: Your Application │ ┌───────────┴───────────┐ │ │ Frontend Backend │ │ │ ├── Order Service │ ├── Payment Service │ └── Database │ │ │ ▼ │ Payment Gateway │ │ │◄──── Checkout UI ───────────┤ │ │ │ Webhook / Status │◄────────────────────────────┘ The key principle is: Frontend initiates the payment experience; backend creates and verifies the payment; the payment gateway is the source of truth for payment status. 1. End-to-End Flow Suppose a customer buys a product worth ₹2,500. Frontend │ │ 1. Create order ▼ Your Backend │ │ 2. Create order in DB │ │ 3. Create payment with gateway ▼ Payment Gateway │ │ 4. Return checkout/payment reference ▼ Your Backend │ │ 5. Send checkout information ▼ Frontend │ │ 6. Open gateway checkout ▼ Customer │ │ 7. Completes payment ▼ Payment Gateway │ ├──────────────► Frontend callback │ └──────────────► Backend webhook │ ▼ Verify │ ▼ Update Order 2. API Responsibilities Frontend APIs The frontend should communicate with your backend, not directly with secret gateway APIs. POST /api/orders POST /api/payments GET /api/payments/{paymentId} The backend communicates with the payment gateway using its secret credentials. 3. Create the Order First Frontend: httpPOST /api/orders Content-Type: application/json Authorization: Bearer <user-token> JSON{ "items": [ { "productId": 101, "quantity": 2 } ], "shippingAddressId": 5 } Backend should calculate the price using its own database. Do not trust: JSON{ "amount": 2500 } from the frontend as the authoritative amount. Instead: Frontend │ │ product IDs + quantities ▼ Backend │ ├── Fetch products ├── Verify prices ├── Verify inventory ├── Calculate total └── Create order Example database state: Order -------------------------------- id = 5001 user_id = 101 amount = 2500 status = PENDING_PAYMENT 4. Create Payment After creating the order: httpPOST /api/payments Backend: Order 5001 │ │ amount = ₹2500 ▼ Payment Service │ │ gateway API ▼ Payment Gateway The gateway might return something like: JSON{ "paymentId": "pay_abc123", "checkoutToken": "..." } Your backend stores the gateway reference: Payment -------------------------------- id = 7001 order_id = 5001 gateway_id = pay_abc123 amount = 2500 status = CREATED The frontend receives only the information it needs to open the checkout. 5. Frontend Opens the Payment UI The frontend might receive: JSON{ "orderId": 5001, "paymentId": "pay_abc123", "checkoutToken": "..." } It then uses the payment provider's client SDK/checkout interface. Conceptually: JavaScriptconst paymentOptions = { paymentId: "pay_abc123", checkoutToken: "..." }; paymentGateway.open(paymentOptions); The exact SDK/API depends on the gateway. 6. Don't Trust the Frontend's Success Callback This is one of the most important parts. Suppose the frontend says: JavaScriptpaymentSuccessful(); You shouldn't immediately mark the order as paid. A malicious client could potentially call the same frontend code without paying. Instead: Frontend says: "Payment succeeded" │ ▼ Backend │ ▼ Verify with gateway │ ├── Confirmed → PAID │ └── Not confirmed → Don't mark as paid 7. Webhooks The payment gateway should notify your backend: httpPOST /api/webhooks/payment Example: JSON{ "event": "payment.success", "paymentId": "pay_abc123", "orderId": "5001", "amount": 2500 } Your backend: Payment Gateway │ │ Webhook ▼ POST /api/webhooks/payment │ ▼ Verify webhook signature │ ▼ Find payment │ ▼ Check amount/order/reference │ ▼ Update payment │ ▼ Update order For example: Payment.status = SUCCESS Order.status = CONFIRMED 8. Payment State Machine Don't simply use: PAID / NOT PAID A better model is: ┌──────────────┐ │ CREATED │ └──────┬───────┘ │ ▼ ┌──────────────┐ │ PENDING │ └──────┬───────┘ │ ┌────────┴────────┐ ▼ ▼ SUCCESS FAILED │ ▼ PAID You might also have: CANCELLED EXPIRED REFUNDED PARTIALLY_REFUNDED This makes payment handling much easier to reason about. 9. Idempotency Payment APIs must handle duplicate requests safely. Imagine the customer clicks: Pay Pay Pay or the network retries a request. Without protection: Request 1 → ₹2500 payment Request 2 → ₹2500 payment Potentially causing two charges. Use an idempotency key: httpIdempotency-Key: order-5001-payment The backend/gateway can recognize that repeated requests represent the same operation. Conceptually: Request │ ▼ Idempotency Key │ ├── First request → Process │ └── Duplicate → Return existing result Your payment creation logic should therefore be designed so that retries don't accidentally create multiple payments. 10. Security Architecture Keep credentials on the server: Frontend │ │ Public/client configuration ▼ Backend │ │ SECRET API KEY ▼ Payment Gateway Never put: SECRET_KEY PRIVATE_KEY GATEWAY_SECRET inside frontend JavaScript. Use environment/secret management: envPAYMENT_GATEWAY_KEY=... PAYMENT_GATEWAY_SECRET=... WEBHOOK_SECRET=... Also use: HTTPS authentication/authorization webhook signature verification server-side amount calculation input validation rate limiting where appropriate audit logs without storing sensitive payment data unnecessarily 11. Suggested API Design /api/v1 │ ├── /orders │ ├── POST / │ └── GET /{orderId} │ ├── /payments │ ├── POST / │ ├── GET /{paymentId} │ └── POST /{paymentId}/refund │ └── /webhooks └── POST /payment Create order httpPOST /api/v1/orders Create payment httpPOST /api/v1/payments Check payment httpGET /api/v1/payments/pay_abc123 Refund httpPOST /api/v1/payments/pay_abc123/refund Gateway webhook httpPOST /api/v1/webhooks/payment The webhook is called by the gateway, not by your frontend. 12. Handling Failures Your integration should explicitly handle: Frontend │ ▼ Backend │ ├── Gateway timeout ├── Gateway unavailable ├── Payment declined ├── Invalid response ├── Duplicate request ├── Webhook delivered twice └── Webhook arrives late For example: Payment request │ ▼ Gateway timeout │ ▼ Payment remains PENDING │ ▼ Webhook/status reconciliation │ ├── SUCCESS → PAID └── FAILED → FAILED Don't automatically assume a timeout means the payment failed. The gateway may have processed the payment even though your request timed out. 13. Recommended Backend Architecture FRONTEND │ ▼ ┌─────────────┐ │ API Router │ └──────┬──────┘ │ ┌─────────┴─────────┐ ▼ ▼ Order Service Payment Service │ │ │ ├── Gateway Client │ │ ▼ ▼ Database Third-party Gateway │ │ Webhook ▼ Webhook Handler │ ▼ Payment Service │ ▼ Database The Payment Service should own payment-specific business logic rather than putting gateway calls directly inside controllers. 14. The Most Important Design Rules ConcernStrategyAmountCalculate on backendGateway secretBackend onlyCheckoutGateway SDK/UIPayment confirmationBackend verification/webhookDuplicate requestsIdempotencyWebhook securityVerify signaturePayment statusExplicit state machineGateway timeoutDon't blindly mark failedDatabaseStore gateway/payment referencesSensitive payment dataMinimize storage; follow gateway/PCI requirementsRefundsBackend-controlled operationAuditabilityRecord payment events/status changes Final mental model FRONTEND │ "I want to buy X" │ ▼ BACKEND │ Calculate + validate │ ▼ CREATE PAYMENT │ ▼ PAYMENT GATEWAY │ Customer pays │ ┌──────┴──────┐ │ │ ▼ ▼ Frontend Webhook callback │ │ ▼ │ Verify signature │ │ └──────► Backend │ ▼ Update Payment │ ▼ Update Order The core security boundary is the backend: the frontend can request a payment, but the backend decides whether an order is actually considered paid based on trusted gateway information.

prompt: Write a FastAPI endpoint that validates and processes file uploads.
response: Below is a production-oriented FastAPI file-upload endpoint that validates file type, size, filename, and content before saving the file. Project structurefile-upload-api/ │ ├── main.py ├── uploads/ └── requirements.txtInstall dependenciespip install fastapi uvicorn python-multipartpython-multipart is required by FastAPI for handling multipart/form-data file uploads.main.pyfrom pathlib import Path import uuid from fastapi import FastAPI, UploadFile, File, HTTPException app = FastAPI() # ========================================== # Configuration # ========================================== UPLOAD_DIR = Path("uploads") MAX_FILE_SIZE = 5 * 1024 * 1024 # 5 MB ALLOWED_EXTENSIONS = { ".jpg", ".jpeg", ".png", ".pdf" } ALLOWED_CONTENT_TYPES = { "image/jpeg", "image/png", "application/pdf" } UPLOAD_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True) # ========================================== # File Upload Endpoint # ========================================== @app.post("/api/files/upload") async def upload_file( file: UploadFile = File(...) ): # -------------------------------------- # 1. Validate filename # -------------------------------------- if not file.filename: raise HTTPException( status_code=400, detail="Filename is required" ) # -------------------------------------- # 2. Validate extension # -------------------------------------- original_filename = Path(file.filename) extension = original_filename.suffix.lower() if extension not in ALLOWED_EXTENSIONS: raise HTTPException( status_code=400, detail="Unsupported file extension" ) # -------------------------------------- # 3. Validate MIME type # -------------------------------------- if file.content_type not in ALLOWED_CONTENT_TYPES: raise HTTPException( status_code=400, detail="Unsupported file type" ) # -------------------------------------- # 4. Generate a safe filename # -------------------------------------- generated_filename = ( f"{uuid.uuid4()}{extension}" ) file_path = UPLOAD_DIR / generated_filename # -------------------------------------- # 5. Read and validate size # -------------------------------------- try: contents = await file.read() if len(contents) > MAX_FILE_SIZE: raise HTTPException( status_code=413, detail="File is too large. Maximum size is 5 MB." ) # ---------------------------------- # 6. Save file # ---------------------------------- with open(file_path, "wb") as buffer: buffer.write(contents) finally: await file.close() # -------------------------------------- # 7. Return response # -------------------------------------- return { "message": "File uploaded successfully", "original_filename": file.filename, "stored_filename": generated_filename, "content_type": file.content_type, "size": len(contents) }RequestThe client sends a multipart/form-data request:POST /api/files/upload Content-Type: multipart/form-dataFor example, using curl:curl -X POST \ http://localhost:8000/api/files/upload \ -F "file=@photo.jpg"The server validates: Uploaded File │ ▼ Filename exists? │ │ NO YES │ │ 400 ▼ Extension valid? │ │ NO YES │ │ 400 ▼ MIME type valid? │ │ NO YES │ │ 400 ▼ Size <= 5 MB? │ │ NO YES │ │ 413 ▼ Generate safe name │ ▼ Save file │ ▼ Success responseWhy generate a new filename?Don't directly save:file.filenamebecause the client controls that value.Instead:generated_filename = f"{uuid.uuid4()}{extension}"produces something like:8f6a2c91-7c4e-4e2f-a0c2-91f9e3d2c112.jpgThis prevents filename collisions and avoids trusting user-controlled filenames for filesystem paths.Running the APIuvicorn main:app --reloadOpen:http://localhost:8000/docsFastAPI automatically provides Swagger UI where you can test the upload endpoint.Important production considerationsThe example above is suitable for learning, but a production upload service should go further.1. Don't rely only on the MIME typeThis:file.content_typecomes from the request and should not be treated as proof of the file's actual contents.For sensitive applications, inspect the file signature/content using an appropriate file-type library.For example:claimed type: image/jpeg actual content: executableshould be rejected.2. Avoid loading huge files into memoryThe example uses:contents = await file.read()which loads the entire file into memory.For large uploads, stream the file in chunks and enforce the size limit while reading:Upload │ ├── chunk 1 ├── chunk 2 ├── chunk 3 └── ... │ ▼ size limit │ ▼ storage3. Use object storageFor production systems, instead of:FastAPI server │ ▼ local uploads/you'll commonly use:FastAPI │ ▼ Object Storage │ ├── Amazon S3 ├── Google Cloud Storage └── Azure Blob Storage4. Consider malware scanningFor user-provided documents:Upload ↓ Validate ↓ Malware scan ↓ Store ↓ Mark file as available5. Store metadata separatelyA database record might contain:File -------------------------------- id original_filename stored_filename content_type size storage_key uploaded_by created_at scan_statusThe actual file can live in object storage.Key ideaA file-upload endpoint isn't simply:await file.read()and save.A safer pipeline is:Request ↓ Filename validation ↓ Extension validation ↓ MIME/content validation ↓ Size validation ↓ Safe generated filename ↓ Malware/content scanning ↓ Storage ↓ Metadata in database ↓ ResponseFor production, validate the file's actual content, enforce limits while streaming, avoid trusting client-provided filenames/types, and preferably store uploaded files outside the application server's local filesystem.Add a streaming upload implementationAdd tests for validation failuresAdd actual content-signature validation

prompt: Explain the difference between authentication and authorization in a backend system.
response: Authentication vs Authorization They are closely related but solve two different problems: Authentication = Who are you? Authorization = What are you allowed to do? Think of entering a college building: You arrive │ ▼ "Who are you?" │ ▼ Show college ID │ ▼ AUTHENTICATION │ ▼ "Okay, you're Rahul." │ ▼ "What are you allowed to access?" │ ▼ Student areas only │ ▼ AUTHORIZATION 1. Authentication Authentication verifies the identity of a user. Common methods: Username + password OTP JWT Session cookies OAuth Biometrics Multi-factor authentication Example: httpPOST /api/login JSON{ "email": "rahul@example.com", "password": "********" } The backend verifies: Email exists? ↓ Password matches hash? ↓ YES ↓ Identity verified The server might then issue a JWT: JSON{ "access_token": "eyJhbGciOi..." } The important question authentication answers is: WHO IS THIS USER? 2. Authorization Once the system knows who you are, it determines what you're allowed to do. Suppose: Rahul → normal customer Admin → administrator They might both successfully authenticate, but have different permissions. Authentication │ ▼ User = Rahul │ ▼ Authorization │ ┌─────────┴─────────┐ ▼ ▼ View Products Delete Product │ │ ALLOW DENY For example: httpDELETE /api/products/501 The backend might check: Is user authenticated? │ ▼ Yes │ ▼ Is user an admin? │ │ Yes No │ │ Allow 403 3. HTTP Status Codes Authentication and authorization failures commonly use different status codes. 401 Unauthorized Usually means: The request doesn't have valid authentication credentials. Example: httpGET /api/profile without a valid token: JSON{ "message": "Authentication required" } 403 Forbidden Usually means: The server knows who you are, but you don't have permission to perform this operation. Example: Authenticated user → Customer Requested operation → Delete another user's account Response: JSON{ "message": "Insufficient permissions" } 4. Backend Example Imagine an Express.js API. Authentication middleware JavaScriptfunction authenticate(req, res, next) { const token = req.headers.authorization; if (!token) { return res.status(401).json({ message: "Authentication required" }); } // Verify token... req.user = { id: 101, role: "customer" }; next(); } This answers: Who is making the request? ↓ User 101 Authorization middleware JavaScriptfunction requireAdmin(req, res, next) { if (req.user.role !== "admin") { return res.status(403).json({ message: "Admin access required" }); } next(); } Now combine them: JavaScriptapp.delete( "/api/products/:id", authenticate, requireAdmin, deleteProduct ); The request passes through: Request │ ▼ Authentication │ │ Who are you? ▼ req.user │ ▼ Authorization │ │ Are you allowed? ▼ Controller │ ▼ Delete product 5. Role-Based Authorization A common authorization model is RBAC — Role-Based Access Control. For example: RoleView ProductsCreate ProductDelete ProductManage UsersCustomer✓✗✗✗Seller✓✓Own products✗Admin✓✓✓✓ The authentication system establishes: JSON{ "userId": 101, "role": "seller" } Authorization then uses the role to determine what operations are permitted. 6. Authentication Doesn't Automatically Mean Authorization This is an important security concept. Suppose a user successfully logs in: Login ↓ Password verified ↓ JWT issued ↓ Authenticated That doesn't mean they can access every API. For example: httpGET /api/admin/users The backend should still check: Valid authentication? ↓ YES ↓ Admin permission? ↓ NO ↓ 403 7. Real-World Example Consider an e-commerce application. Authentication Rahul logs in: Email + Password ↓ Password verification ↓ JWT ↓ Rahul authenticated Authorization Rahul requests: httpGET /api/orders/5001 Backend checks: Is Rahul authenticated? ↓ YES ↓ Does order 5001 belong to Rahul? ↓ YES ↓ ALLOW But if Rahul requests another customer's order: GET /api/orders/9001 the backend should reject it even though Rahul is authenticated. This is authorization based on resource ownership. 8. The Complete Security Flow HTTP Request │ ▼ ┌─────────────────┐ │ Authentication │ │ │ │ Who are you? │ └────────┬────────┘ │ ┌─────┴─────┐ │ │ Invalid Valid │ │ 401 ▼ ┌─────────────────┐ │ Authorization │ │ │ │ What can you │ │ do? │ └────────┬────────┘ │ ┌─────┴─────┐ │ │ Denied Allowed │ │ 403 ▼ Controller │ ▼ Database The simplest way to remember it AuthenticationAuthorizationQuestionWho are you?What can you do?HappensFirstAfter authenticationExampleLogin/passwordRole/permission checkCommon technologiesJWT, sessions, OAuthRBAC, ABAC, permissionsFailureUsually 401Usually 403 Key idea: Authentication establishes identity; authorization uses that identity (and often roles, permissions, ownership, or policies) to decide access.

prompt: Design a full-stack application architecture connecting a React frontend to a FastAPI backend.
response: Full-Stack Architecture: React + FastAPI A clean production-oriented architecture separates the frontend, API/backend, business logic, and data layer. USERS │ ▼ ┌─────────────┐ │ React │ │ Frontend │ └──────┬──────┘ │ HTTPS / JSON │ ▼ ┌─────────────┐ │ FastAPI │ │ API │ └──────┬──────┘ │ ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ Auth Service Business Validation Logic │ │ └─────────────┼─────────────┘ ▼ ┌─────────────┐ │ Repository │ │ / ORM │ └──────┬──────┘ │ ▼ ┌─────────────┐ │ PostgreSQL │ └─────────────┘ 1. React Frontend The React application is responsible for: UI components Pages/routes User interactions Form handling Client-side validation Calling FastAPI Managing UI state Displaying loading/error states Authentication state A reasonable structure is: frontend/ │ ├── src/ │ ├── components/ │ ├── pages/ │ ├── layouts/ │ ├── hooks/ │ ├── services/ │ │ └── api.js │ ├── context/ │ ├── utils/ │ └── App.jsx │ └── package.json For example: JavaScript// services/api.js export async function getProducts() { const response = await fetch( "http://localhost:8000/api/v1/products" ); if (!response.ok) { throw new Error("Failed to fetch products"); } return response.json(); } The components shouldn't contain lots of raw API URLs. Keep API communication in a service layer. 2. FastAPI Backend The FastAPI application exposes REST endpoints: /api/v1 │ ├── /auth ├── /users ├── /products ├── /orders └── /payments A clean backend structure: backend/ │ ├── app/ │ ├── main.py │ │ │ ├── routers/ │ │ ├── auth.py │ │ ├── users.py │ │ ├── products.py │ │ └── orders.py │ │ │ ├── schemas/ │ │ ├── user.py │ │ ├── product.py │ │ └── order.py │ │ │ ├── models/ │ │ ├── user.py │ │ ├── product.py │ │ └── order.py │ │ │ ├── services/ │ │ ├── auth.py │ │ ├── product.py │ │ └── order.py │ │ │ ├── repositories/ │ │ └── ... │ │ │ ├── database/ │ │ └── connection.py │ │ │ └── middleware/ │ └── ... │ └── requirements.txt 3. Request Flow Suppose the user opens a product page.
