prompt: Explain promises, async/await, and fetch in JavaScript using a weather API example.
response: Promises, async/await, and fetch() in JavaScript These three concepts are commonly used together when JavaScript needs to get data from a server or API. A simple way to remember them: Promise = represents future result fetch() = requests data from a server async/await = makes Promise-based code easier to read 1. What is a Promise? A Promise represents the eventual result of an asynchronous operation. A Promise has three states: Pending │ ├──→ Fulfilled (success) │ └──→ Rejected (failure) For example: JavaScriptconst promise = fetch("https://example.com/data"); The fetch() function doesn't immediately give you the response data. It returns a Promise. You can handle it using .then() and .catch(): JavaScriptfetch("https://example.com/data") .then(response => response.json()) .then(data => { console.log(data); }) .catch(error => { console.error(error); }); .then() Runs when the Promise succeeds. .catch() Runs when an error occurs. 2. What is async/await? async/await provides a cleaner way to work with Promises. The same example can be written as: JavaScriptasync function getData() { try { const response = await fetch("https://example.com/data"); const data = await response.json(); console.log(data); } catch (error) { console.error(error); } } getData(); async An async function automatically returns a Promise. JavaScriptasync function hello() { return "Hello"; } await await waits for a Promise to settle inside an async function. JavaScriptconst response = await fetch(url); It makes asynchronous code easier to read, although JavaScript itself remains asynchronous. 3. What is fetch()? fetch() is a browser API used to make HTTP requests. For example: JavaScriptconst response = await fetch("https://example.com/weather"); The basic flow is: JavaScript │ │ fetch() ↓ Weather API │ │ JSON response ↓ JavaScript │ ↓ Display weather 4. Weather API Example Suppose a weather service provides an endpoint like: https://api.example.com/weather?city=Hyderabad The API might return JSON such as: JSON{ "city": "Hyderabad", "temperature": 29, "humidity": 65, "condition": "Cloudy" } We can retrieve it using fetch(). 5. Using Promises with a Weather API JavaScriptconst url = "https://api.example.com/weather?city=Hyderabad"; fetch(url) .then(response => response.json()) .then(data => { console.log("City:", data.city); console.log("Temperature:", data.temperature); console.log("Condition:", data.condition); }) .catch(error => { console.error("Error:", error); }); The sequence is: fetch() ↓ Promise ↓ response.json() ↓ Promise

Using Promises with a Weather API JavaScriptconst url = "https://api.example.com/weather?city=Hyderabad"; fetch(url) .then(response => response.json()) .then(data => { console.log("City:", data.city); console.log("Temperature:", data.temperature); console.log("Condition:", data.condition); }) .catch(error => { console.error("Error:", error); }); The sequence is: fetch() ↓ Promise ↓ response.json() ↓ Promise

React Hooks: useState and useEffect Hooks are special React functions that let functional components use features such as state and side effects. The two most commonly used hooks are: useState() → stores and updates component data useEffect() → performs side effects after rendering 1. useState() useState() lets a component remember a value between renders. Syntax JavaScriptconst [state, setState] = useState(initialValue); For example: JavaScriptimport { useState } from "react"; function Counter() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0); return (

Count: {count}

); } Here: PartMeaningcountCurrent valuesetCountFunction that updates the value0Initial value When the button is clicked: Click button ↓ setCount(count + 1) ↓ State changes ↓ React re-renders component ↓ New count displayed 2. Practical useState() Example: Form Input State can also control form fields. JavaScriptimport { useState } from "react"; function UserForm() { const [name, setName] = useState(""); return (
setName(event.target.value)} placeholder="Enter your name" />

Hello, {name}

); } If the user types: Alice the state becomes: JavaScriptname = "Alice" and React updates: Hello, Alice 3. What is useEffect()? useEffect() is used for side effects. A side effect is an operation that interacts with something outside the component's normal rendering process. Common examples: Fetching data from an API Updating the document title Setting up timers Subscribing to events Working with browser APIs Basic syntax JavaScriptuseEffect(() => { // side effect }, []); The first argument is the function containing the effect. The second argument is the dependency array. 4. useEffect() with an Empty Dependency Array Consider: JavaScriptimport { useEffect } from "react"; function App() { useEffect(() => { console.log("Component loaded"); }, []); return

Hello React

; } The empty array: JavaScript[] means the effect doesn't depend on changing state or props, so React runs it after the component's initial mount. A common example is fetching initial data. 5. Practical Example: Fetching API Data JavaScriptimport { useState, useEffect } from "react"; function Users() { const [users, setUsers] = useState([]); useEffect(() => { fetch("https://example.com/api/users") .then(response => response.json()) .then(data => { setUsers(data); }); }, []); return (

Users

    {users.map(user => (
  • {user.name}
    • ))}
); } The sequence is: Component renders ↓ useEffect runs ↓ fetch API ↓ Receive data ↓ setUsers(data) ↓ State changes ↓ Component re-renders ↓ Users displayed 6. Dependency Array The dependency array controls when the effect runs again. No dependency array JavaScriptuseEffect(() => { console.log("Effect runs after every render"); }); It runs after every render. Empty dependency array JavaScriptuseEffect(() => { console.log("Effect runs after initial mount"); }, []); It doesn't rerun because of later state/prop changes. Dependency included JavaScriptuseEffect(() => { console.log("Count changed"); }, [count]); The effect runs after the initial mount and whenever count changes. For example: JavaScriptfunction Counter() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0); useEffect(() => { document.title = `Count: ${count}`; }, [count]); return ( ); } If count becomes 5, the browser tab title becomes: Count: 5 7. useEffect() Cleanup Some effects create resources that need to be cleaned up. For example, a timer: JavaScriptimport { useEffect } from "react"; function Timer() { useEffect(() => { const timer = setInterval(() => { console.log("Timer running"); }, 1000); return () => { clearInterval(timer); }; }, []); return

; } The function returned from the effect is the cleanup function. Component starts ↓ setInterval() ↓ Timer runs ↓ Component unmounts ↓ clearInterval() Cleanup is important for timers, subscriptions, event listeners, and similar resources. 8. useState + useEffect Together A practical example is a simple counter whose document title updates automatically. import { useState, useEffect } from "react"; function Counter() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0); useEffect(() => { document.title = `Count: ${count}`; }, [count]); return (

Counter

); } export default Counter; Here: useState ↓ Stores count ↓ Button changes count ↓ Component re-renders ↓ useEffect ↓ Updates document title 9. Important Rules of Hooks Hooks have some important rules. 1. Call Hooks at the top level Do: JavaScriptfunction App() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0); } Don't put Hooks inside conditions: JavaScript// ❌ Don't do this if (loggedIn) { const [name, setName] = useState(""); } 2. Don't call Hooks inside loops JavaScript// ❌ Don't do this for (...) { useState(...); } 3. Call Hooks from React functions Hooks should generally be called from: React function components Custom Hooks 10. useState vs useEffect HookPurposeExampleuseStateStore changing dataCounteruseEffectPerform side effectsAPI requestuseStateForm valuesInput fielduseEffectUpdate document titledocument.titleuseStateStore API resultsUser listuseEffectFetch API datafetch() Easy exam memory useState = remember data useEffect = do something after rendering Typical pattern: JavaScriptconst [data, setData] = useState([]); useEffect(() => { // Fetch or synchronize something }, []); Key takeaway: useState() manages a component's changing data, while useEffect() is used to synchronize the component with external systems such as APIs, timers, subscriptions, or browser APIs.

prompt: Explain the differences between client-side rendering, server-side rendering, and static generation in Next.js.
response:
Rendering in Next.js Next.js supports several ways to generate the HTML for a page. The three important concepts are: Client-Side Rendering (CSR) Server-Side Rendering (SSR) Static Generation (SSG) The main difference is where and when the HTML is generated. 1. Client-Side Rendering (CSR) In Client-Side Rendering, the browser receives a relatively minimal HTML page and JavaScript. React then runs in the browser and generates/updates the UI. Flow Browser │ │ Request ↓ Next.js Server │ │ HTML + JavaScript ↓ Browser │ │ React runs ↓ UI displayed/updated Example In the App Router, a component using client-only state/interactivity might be: JavaScript"use client"; import { useState } from "react"; export default function Counter() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0); return ( ); } The "use client" directive makes the component a Client Component, allowing browser-side features such as state and event handlers. Good for Interactive dashboards Forms Shopping carts Components requiring browser APIs Highly interactive UI Advantage After the application is loaded, interactions can be very dynamic without requesting a new HTML page for every interaction. Disadvantage The initial experience can depend more heavily on JavaScript loading/execution, and purely client-fetched data isn't available in the initial server-generated HTML. 2. Server-Side Rendering (SSR) With Server-Side Rendering, the server generates HTML for a request and sends that HTML to the browser. Conceptually: Browser │ │ Request /products ↓ Server │ │ Fetch data │ Generate HTML ↓ Browser │ ↓ Rendered page For example, a server-rendered page might retrieve current product information before returning the page. In modern Next.js App Router, Server Components are the default, and dynamic server rendering can be used when the page needs request-time data or other dynamic behavior. A simplified example: JavaScriptexport default async function ProductsPage() { const response = await fetch( "https://api.example.com/products", { cache: "no-store" } ); const products = await response.json(); return (

Products

{products.map(product => (

{product.name}

))}
); } The important idea is that the data is obtained on the server for the request, rather than waiting for browser-side JavaScript to fetch it. Good for Frequently changing data Personalized pages Request-specific information Pages where fresh server data is important Advantage The browser can receive meaningful HTML containing the requested data without having to perform the initial data fetch itself. Disadvantage The server has to do work when the page is requested, so it can require more server resources than a pre-generated static page. 3. Static Generation (SSG) Static Generation means the HTML is generated ahead of time rather than generated for every request. Conceptually: Build time │ │ Generate HTML ↓ Static files │ │ Request ↓ Browser For example, suppose you have a documentation website where the content changes only occasionally. Next.js can generate the pages ahead of time and serve them as static output. Build ↓ /about.html /products.html /contact.html ↓ Users request pages ↓ Static HTML served Good for Blogs Documentation Marketing pages Product information that doesn't change frequently Portfolios Advantages Fast delivery Can be served efficiently from a CDN No server-side rendering required for every request Good scalability Disadvantage If the underlying data changes, the generated page needs to be regenerated or revalidated. 4. Main Difference FeatureCSRSSRSSGRendering locationBrowserServerBuild timeWhen HTML is generatedIn browserPer requestDuring buildData fetchingBrowser commonly fetches dataServer can fetch per requestUsually fetched/generated ahead of timeFreshnessCan be very freshVery freshDepends on regeneration/revalidationServer work per requestLower for renderingHigherVery lowGood forInteractive appsDynamic pagesStatic/content sitesCDN-friendlyYes, depending on architectureSomewhatExcellent 5. Simple Example Imagine a news website. CSR Request page ↓ Browser gets app ↓ JavaScript requests news ↓ News displayed SSR Request page ↓ Server gets latest news ↓ Server creates HTML ↓ Browser receives news page SSG Build website ↓ Generate news page ↓ Store generated page ↓ Users receive generated page 6. Important Next.js Point Modern Next.js makes the distinction a little more nuanced than older tutorials suggest. With the App Router: Server Components are the default. Server Components can fetch data on the server. A route can be statically rendered or dynamically rendered depending on its data and configuration. Client Components are used when you need browser-side interactivity such as useState, event handlers, or browser APIs. Static pages can also use revalidation so they aren't necessarily permanently frozen. So don't think of Next.js as simply: Next.js = SSR Instead, think: Next.js │ ┌────────────┼────────────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ CSR SSR SSG Browser Request Build And in a real application, these approaches can be combined. For example: Product page │ ├── Product information → Server-rendered/static │ ├── Product reviews → Server/data fetching │ └── Add to Cart button → Client Component That combination is one of the major strengths of Next.js. Easy exam memory CSR → Browser renders SSR → Server renders per request SSG → Build process renders ahead of time Or simply: CSR = Render in Browser SSR = Render on Request SSG = Render at Build Time

prompt: Explain frontend architecture patterns for scaling a large React application.

Frontend Architecture Patterns for Large React Applications As a React application grows, putting everything into App.jsx becomes difficult to maintain. A large application needs a clear architecture that separates UI, business logic, data access, and shared functionality. A useful way to think about it is: Large React Application │ ├── UI Components ├── Features / Business Logic ├── Pages / Routing ├── State Management ├── API / Data Layer ├── Shared Utilities └── Configuration 1. Component-Based Architecture React itself encourages component-based architecture. Instead of creating one huge component: App.jsx ├── 500 lines ├── Forms ├── API calls ├── Tables ├── Modals └── Business logic split it into smaller components: App │ ├── Navbar ├── Sidebar ├── Dashboard │ ├── StatisticsCard │ ├── SalesChart │ └── RecentOrders └── Footer Example: JavaScriptfunction Dashboard() { return (
); } Benefits Reusable Easier to test Easier to understand Easier to maintain 2. Feature-Based Architecture For a large application, organizing everything by technical type can become difficult. For example: components/ hooks/ services/ utils/ can eventually contain hundreds of unrelated files. A feature-based approach groups code by business feature: src/ ├── features/ │ ├── auth/ │ │ ├── components/ │ │ ├── hooks/ │ │ ├── services/ │ │ └── authSlice.js │ │ │ ├── products/ │ │ ├── components/ │ │ ├── hooks/ │ │ └── productApi.js │ │ │ └── orders/ │ ├── components/ │ ├── hooks/ │ └── orderApi.js │ ├── shared/ │ ├── components/ │ ├── hooks/ │ └── utils/ │ └── App.jsx This is often easier to scale because everything related to a feature is located together. Example The products feature might contain: products/ ├── components/ │ ├── ProductCard.jsx │ └── ProductList.jsx ├── hooks/ │ └── useProducts.js └── productApi.js 3. Layered Architecture Another approach is separating the application into layers. ┌─────────────────────────────┐ │ Presentation │ │ React Components │ ├─────────────────────────────┤ │ Business Logic │ │ Hooks / Services │ ├─────────────────────────────┤ │ Data Layer │ │ API / State Store │ ├─────────────────────────────┤ │ External Systems │ │ Backend / APIs │ └─────────────────────────────┘ For example: ProductList.jsx ↓ useProducts() ↓ productService.js ↓ HTTP API ↓ Backend This prevents UI components from becoming tightly coupled to API implementation details. 4. Separate UI from Business Logic Avoid putting a large amount of business logic directly inside JSX. Harder to maintain JavaScriptfunction Product() { // Lots of API calls // Validation // Calculations // State management // UI // ... return
...
; } Instead, extract logic into a custom Hook: JavaScriptfunction useProduct(productId) { // Fetch and manage product data } Then the component focuses on presentation: JavaScriptfunction ProductPage({ productId }) { const { product, loading } = useProduct(productId); if (loading) { return

; } return ; } This creates a cleaner separation: Component → UI Hook → Logic Service → API communication 5. State Management Architecture Large React applications usually have different kinds of state. Local UI state Examples: Modal open/closed Input value Selected tab Use: JavaScriptuseState() Shared client state Examples: Authentication information Shopping cart Application preferences Depending on the application, tools such as Redux Toolkit, Zustand, or Context can be used. Server state Examples: Products from an API Orders User profiles This is often better handled with a server-state/data-fetching library such as TanStack Query rather than putting every API response into a global client store. A useful distinction is: State │ ├── Local UI state │ └── useState │ ├── Shared client state │ └── Redux/Zustand/etc. │ └── Server state └── Data-fetching/cache library 6. Shared Component Architecture Large applications often need reusable components: shared/ ├── components/ │ ├── Button/ │ ├── Modal/ │ ├── Input/ │ ├── Table/ │ └── LoadingSpinner/ │ ├── hooks/ │ ├── useDebounce.js │ └── useLocalStorage.js │ └── utils/ ├── formatDate.js └── validation.js For example: JavaScript Instead of implementing button styling repeatedly throughout the application. 7. Container and Presentational Pattern A traditional React pattern separates: Container Handles data and logic. JavaScriptfunction UserContainer() { const users = useUsers(); return ; } Presentational component Focuses on displaying data. JavaScriptfunction UserList({ users }) { return (

  • {user.name}
