Example Production Architecture PDF ↓ Document Parser ↓ ───────────────── Text Tables Images Code ───────────────── ↓ Specialized Processing ↓ Embeddings ↓ Vector Store ↓ Retriever ↓ Reranker ↓ LLM Summary For high-quality RAG systems: Tables Preserve row/column structure. Avoid splitting tables arbitrarily. Store table metadata. Images Extract captions. Use OCR for embedded text. Generate image descriptions with vision models. Consider multimodal embeddings when needed. Code Blocks Preserve formatting exactly. Chunk code separately from prose. Store language metadata. Keep explanatory context nearby. A useful rule is: Treat tables, images, code, and prose as different content types during ingestion rather than flattening everything into plain text. Doing so usually produces significantly better retrieval recall, more accurate answers, and more reliable citations in document-question-answering systems.

prompt: Explain the difference between sparse, dense, and multi-vector retrieval such as ColBERT.
response: When building a retrieval system, one of the most important design choices is how documents and queries are represented. Modern retrieval approaches generally fall into three categories: Sparse retrieval (e.g., BM25) Dense retrieval (single-vector embeddings) Multi-vector retrieval (e.g., ColBERT) Each makes different trade-offs between accuracy, efficiency, interpretability, and storage. The Core Retrieval Problem Suppose a user asks: How do I recover my account password? And a document contains: Credential recovery procedure for account access. A retrieval system must recognize that these are related even though they use different words. The main difference between sparse, dense, and multi-vector methods is how they represent meaning. Sparse Retrieval Sparse retrieval represents text as a very large vector where most entries are zero. Example document: password recovery procedure Vocabulary: password recovery procedure account login ... Representation: password = 1 recovery = 1 procedure = 1 account = 0 login = 0 ... Most dimensions are: 0 Hence the name sparse. BM25: The Most Common Sparse Method BM25 ranks documents using: Term frequency Document frequency Document length normalization Example: Query: password recovery Document A: password recovery guide Document B: network configuration manual BM25 gives Document A a much higher score. Advantages of Sparse Retrieval Excellent Keyword Matching Example: ERR_1042 or: Product-XJ900 Sparse retrieval handles exact identifiers very well. Interpretable You can explain: Document matched because it contains: password recovery Fast and Mature Technologies such as: Lucene Elasticsearch OpenSearch have optimized sparse retrieval for years. Weaknesses of Sparse Retrieval Example: Query: password reset Document: credential recovery No overlapping terms. BM25 may miss it entirely. This vocabulary mismatch is the main limitation. Dense Retrieval Dense retrieval uses embeddings. Instead of: Thousands of sparse dimensions we create: One dense vector Example: password reset might become: [0.12, -0.45, 0.89, ...] with every dimension containing a value. Dense Retrieval Workflow Document ↓ Embedding Model ↓ Vector Query ↓ Embedding Model ↓ Vector Similarity is computed using: Cosine similarity Dot product Euclidean distance Why Dense Retrieval Works Example: Query: password reset Document: credential recovery Even though the words differ: password ≈ credential reset ≈ recovery their embeddings may be close. This enables semantic retrieval. Advantages of Dense Retrieval Semantic Understanding Can retrieve: password reset from: credential recovery Better Recall Often finds relevant documents that keyword search misses. Works Across Languages Many multilingual embedding models support: English query ↓ French document retrieval. Weaknesses of Dense Retrieval Exact Matches Can Be Difficult Query: ERR_1042 Dense models may not prioritize exact identifiers. Compression Loss An entire document chunk becomes: One Vector Information is compressed. Some details may be lost. Requires ANN Infrastructure Typically uses: HNSW IVF Vector databases instead of traditional inverted indexes. Single-Vector Limitation Suppose a document contains: Authentication Pricing Troubleshooting API Usage Dense retrieval creates: One Embedding representing all topics. Important details may become diluted. This is called the representation bottleneck. Multi-Vector Retrieval Multi-vector systems address this limitation. Instead of: Document ↓ One Vector they create: Document ↓ Many Vectors Each vector represents a different part of the text. ColBERT Overview ColBERT stands for: Contextualized Late Interaction over BERT It is one of the most influential multi-vector retrieval systems. How ColBERT Represents Text Sentence: password recovery procedure Instead of one embedding: [0.1, 0.4, ...] ColBERT creates: password → vector recovery → vector procedure → vector Every token receives its own representation. Dense Retrieval vs ColBERT Dense retrieval: Document ↓ Single Vector ColBERT: Document ↓ Token Vector 1 Token Vector 2 Token Vector 3 ... This preserves much more information. Late Interaction Traditional dense retrieval: Query Vector vs Document Vector One similarity calculation. ColBERT: Query Tokens ↓ Compare Against Document Tokens ↓ Aggregate Scores The matching occurs after encoding. Hence: Late Interaction Example Query: reset password Document: credential recovery procedure ColBERT compares token-level representations: reset ↔ recovery password ↔ credential and aggregates the matches. This often captures relevance better than a single document embedding. Why ColBERT Improves Retrieval Dense retrieval compresses: 100 tokens into: 1 vector ColBERT preserves: 100 token vectors Much less information is lost. Advantages of ColBERT Higher Recall Often retrieves more relevant documents. Better Precision Especially for: Long documents Technical content Complex questions Strong Semantic Matching Maintains detailed token-level information. Trade-Offs of ColBERT Larger Indexes Instead of: 1 vector per chunk you store: Many vectors per chunk Storage increases substantially. More Complex Infrastructure Search is more expensive than standard dense retrieval. Higher Latency Token-level scoring requires more computation. Comparison Example Document: API authentication and token refresh procedures Query: How do I renew an access token? Sparse Retrieval May fail because: renew and refresh are different words. Dense Retrieval Likely succeeds due to semantic similarity. ColBERT Often performs even better because token-level interactions preserve fine-grained relationships. Hybrid Retrieval Many production systems combine: Sparse + Dense or: Sparse + ColBERT Workflow: BM25 ↓ Top 100 Documents ↓ Dense/ColBERT Reranking ↓ Top Results This frequently outperforms any single method. Storage Comparison Suppose: 1 million documents Sparse Stores: Inverted Index Efficient. Dense Stores: 1 vector per document Moderate storage. ColBERT Stores: Many vectors per document Largest storage footprint. Retrieval Quality Comparison General trend: Sparse < Dense < ColBERT for semantic retrieval tasks. However: Exact keyword search may still favor sparse methods. Typical Use Cases Sparse Retrieval Good for: Enterprise search Product IDs Error codes Legal citations Exact matches Dense Retrieval Good for: RAG systems Semantic search FAQ search Knowledge bases ColBERT Good for: High-quality retrieval Research systems Large document collections Complex semantic search Summary FeatureSparse (BM25)DenseMulti-Vector (ColBERT)RepresentationKeywordsOne embeddingMany embeddingsSemantic understandingLowHighVery highExact matchingExcellentModerateGoodStorage costLowMediumHighRetrieval speedFastFastSlowerRecallModerateHighVery highInfrastructure complexityLowMediumHigh Conceptually: Sparse Query ↔ Keywords Dense Query Vector ↔ Document Vector ColBERT Query Token Vectors ↔ Document Token Vectors The progression is essentially a trade-off between efficiency and representational power. Sparse retrieval excels at exact matching, dense retrieval adds semantic understanding, and multi-vector methods like ColBERT preserve much richer information, often achieving the highest retrieval quality at the cost of additional storage and computation.

prompt: Explain parent-document retrieval and hierarchical chunking strategies.
response: When building a RAG system, one of the biggest challenges is balancing two competing goals: Small chunks retrieve better because they are focused on a single topic. Large chunks answer better because they contain more context. Parent-document retrieval and hierarchical chunking are techniques designed to get the benefits of both. The Chunking Problem Suppose a document contains: Chapter: Authentication Authentication uses OAuth2. Access tokens expire after 60 minutes. Refresh tokens can be used to obtain new access tokens. Administrators may configure expiration policies. ... If you create one large chunk: Entire chapter retrieval may be less precise because the embedding represents many topics. If you create tiny chunks: Chunk 1: Authentication uses OAuth2. Chunk 2: Access tokens expire after 60 minutes. Chunk 3: Refresh tokens can be used... retrieval becomes more precise, but the LLM may not receive enough surrounding context to answer complex questions. Parent-Document Retrieval The key idea: Retrieve small chunks, but return larger chunks. Structure Instead of storing only one chunk size: Document create: Parent Chunk ↓ Child Chunks Example: Parent: Authentication Section Contains: Child 1: Authentication uses OAuth2. Child 2: Access tokens expire after 60 minutes. Child 3: Refresh tokens can be used... Indexing Process Step 1 Split document into large parent chunks. Example: 1000-token parents Step 2 Split each parent into smaller children. Example: 200-token children Step 3 Embed only the children. Parent ↓ Child Chunks ↓ Embeddings Step 4 Store a link: Child ↓ Parent ID Example: JSON{ "child_id": 17, "parent_id": 3 } Retrieval Process User asks: How long do access tokens remain valid? Retrieve: Child: Access tokens expire after 60 minutes. This chunk matches strongly. Instead of returning only that child: Access tokens expire after 60 minutes. retrieve the entire parent: Authentication Section which contains: OAuth2 Token expiration Refresh tokens Policy configuration The LLM receives richer context. Why Parent Retrieval Helps Without parent retrieval: Question ↓ Small Chunk ↓ Limited Context With parent retrieval: Question ↓ Small Chunk Match ↓ Parent Section ↓ More Context This often improves answer quality significantly. Example Question: How do refresh tokens relate to token expiration? A small chunk may contain: Refresh tokens can be used... but not explain expiration. The parent section contains both concepts, allowing a complete answer. Hierarchical Chunking Parent retrieval is a special case of a broader idea: Document ↓ Hierarchy Instead of a single chunk level: Document ↓ Chunks we create multiple levels. Example Hierarchy Document ↓ Chapter ↓ Section ↓ Paragraph For example: API Guide becomes: Chapter: Authentication Section: OAuth2 Paragraph: Access tokens expire... Tree Representation Document ├── Chapter A │ ├── Section A1 │ ├── Section A2 │ └── Section A3 └── Chapter B ├── Section B1 └── Section B2 This structure preserves relationships within the document. Why Hierarchical Chunking Helps Documents naturally have structure: Books Manuals Research papers Policies Contracts Ignoring this structure can hurt retrieval. Consider: Section: Security Requirements Every paragraph within that section shares the same topic. Hierarchical chunking preserves that relationship. Multi-Level Retrieval A query can retrieve at different levels. Example: Question: What are security requirements? Retrieve: Section Level Question: What port number is used? Retrieve: Paragraph Level Different questions benefit from different granularities. Recursive Retrieval Advanced systems perform retrieval in stages. Workflow: Query ↓ Retrieve Chapters ↓ Retrieve Sections ↓ Retrieve Paragraphs Each stage narrows the search. Example: Document ↓ Chapter: Authentication ↓ Section: Token Management ↓ Paragraph: Access tokens expire after 60 minutes Multi-Resolution Retrieval Store embeddings at multiple levels. Example: Chapter Embedding Section Embedding Paragraph Embedding A query can match whichever level is most appropriate. Example Question: Explain the authentication architecture. Likely matches: Chapter Embedding Question: How long does an access token last? Likely matches: Paragraph Embedding Chunk Size Strategy A common hierarchy: Document ↓ 1500-token parent ↓ 300-token child or: Document ↓ Chapter ↓ Section ↓ Paragraph The best sizes depend on the content. Parent Retrieval vs Standard Chunking Standard Chunking Question ↓ Retrieve Chunk ↓ LLM Problem: Chunk may be too small. Parent Retrieval Question ↓ Retrieve Child ↓ Return Parent ↓ LLM Benefit: Higher context quality. Parent Retrieval vs Larger Chunks A tempting alternative is: Just use larger chunks. Example: 1500 tokens However: Larger chunk ↓ Less precise retrieval The embedding must represent many topics. Parent retrieval avoids this trade-off. Typical Production Pipeline Document ↓ Parent Chunks ↓ Child Chunks ↓ Embed Children ↓ Vector Store Retrieval: Query ↓ Match Child ↓ Find Parent ↓ Send Parent to LLM When Parent Retrieval Works Well Especially useful for: Technical documentation Policies Contracts Research papers Books Product manuals These documents have strong hierarchical structure. Potential Downsides Larger Context Sent to LLM Returning parents increases token usage. Example: Child: 200 tokens Parent: 1500 tokens Cost increases. More Storage Metadata Need mappings: Child → Parent for every chunk. More Complex Pipeline Standard retrieval is simpler. Parent retrieval introduces additional logic. Combining With Reranking A common approach: Query ↓ Retrieve Child Chunks ↓ Rerank ↓ Expand to Parents ↓ LLM This improves precision while retaining context. Example Configuration A practical setup might use: Parent Size: 1000–2000 tokens Child Size: 200–400 tokens Child Overlap: 50–100 tokens Retrieve: Top 10 children then return: Top 3–5 parents to the LLM. Summary Parent-document retrieval retrieves small chunks for accuracy but returns larger parent sections for context. Small Child ↓ Retrieval Match ↓ Large Parent ↓ LLM Hierarchical chunking organizes documents into multiple levels such as: Document ↓ Chapter ↓ Section ↓ Paragraph Benefits include: Better retrieval precision Better answer context Preservation of document structure Improved performance on long documents In practice, parent-document retrieval is one of the most effective ways to improve RAG quality because it solves the fundamental tension between retrieval granularity and context richness.

prompt: Explain how to cite sources and provide grounded answers in a RAG application.
response: Providing citations is one of the most important parts of a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system. Citations help users: Verify answers Inspect the original evidence Build trust in the system Distinguish retrieved facts from model-generated text A RAG system should aim to produce grounded answers: answers that are explicitly supported by retrieved source content. What Is a Grounded Answer? A grounded answer is an answer that can be traced back to specific retrieved documents. Example: Question: What is the warranty period? Retrieved text: The warranty covers defects for 24 months from the purchase date. Grounded answer: The warranty period is 24 months from the purchase date. (Source: User Manual, Page 42) Every factual claim can be linked to supporting evidence. Why Grounding Matters Without grounding: Question ↓ LLM ↓ Answer The model may: Hallucinate Misremember facts Mix sources Invent details With grounding: Question ↓ Retrieve Sources ↓ LLM Uses Sources ↓ Answer + Citations The answer is constrained by actual documents. Store Source Metadata During Ingestion When indexing documents, store metadata alongside each chunk. Example: JSON{ "text": "...", "document": "employee_handbook.pdf", "page": 15, "section": "Vacation Policy" } This metadata becomes the basis for citations later. Preserve Document Structure Useful metadata may include: Document Name Page Number Section Title Chapter URL Publication Date Example: JSON{ "source": "security_guide.pdf", "page": 42, "section": "API Authentication" } Retrieve Sources Along With Text Do not retrieve only the text. Bad: Access tokens expire after 60 minutes. Metadata lost. Better: JSON{ "text": "Access tokens expire after 60 minutes.", "page": 42, "document": "security_guide.pdf" } Now the answer can cite the source. Citation Styles Several citation styles work well in RAG. Inline Citations Example: Access tokens expire after 60 minutes (Security Guide, p.42). Simple and easy to read. Bracketed References Example: Access tokens expire after 60 minutes [1]. References: [1] Security Guide, Page 42 Common in enterprise systems. Footnote Style Example: Access tokens expire after 60 minutes¹ Footnote: ¹ Security Guide, Page 42 Hyperlinked Citations If documents are stored online: Access tokens expire after 60 minutes. (Source) Users can open the original document directly. Chunk-Level Citations The most reliable approach is citing the retrieved chunk. Example: Retrieved chunk: Page 42: Access tokens expire after 60 minutes. Answer: Access tokens expire after 60 minutes (Page 42). This keeps citations tightly coupled to evidence. Passage-Level Citations For long documents: Document ↓ Page ↓ Paragraph Store passage identifiers. Example: JSON{ "page": 42, "paragraph": 3 } This gives users more precise references. Multiple Sources Answers often synthesize multiple documents. Example: Question: How does authentication work? Retrieved: Document A: OAuth2 overview Document B: Token expiration policy Answer: Authentication uses OAuth2 [1]. Access tokens expire after 60 minutes [2]. References: [1] Security Architecture Guide [2] Token Management Policy Mapping Claims to Sources A common mistake: Entire answer ↓ One citation This makes verification difficult. Better: Claim A → Source A Claim B → Source B Claim C → Source C Users can trace each statement independently. Prompting the LLM for Grounded Answers Explicit instructions help. Example prompt: Use only the provided context. If the answer is not present, say that the information was not found. Cite supporting sources for every factual claim. This reduces hallucinations. Refuse Unsupported Claims Suppose retrieval returns: No information about warranty length. Bad answer: The warranty is probably 12 months. Hallucinated. Better: The retrieved documents do not specify a warranty period. Grounded systems should prefer uncertainty over invention. Answer Generation Workflow Query ↓ Retriever ↓ Chunks + Metadata ↓ Prompt ↓ LLM ↓ Answer + Citations Metadata flows all the way through the pipeline. Citation-Aware Prompt Example Provide retrieved context like: [Source 1] Document: Security Guide Page: 42 Access tokens expire after 60 minutes. [Source 2] Document: API Manual Page: 88 Refresh tokens can be used to obtain new access tokens. Question: How are tokens managed? The model can generate: Access tokens expire after 60 minutes (Source 1). Refresh tokens can be used to obtain new access tokens (Source 2). Handling Conflicting Sources Sometimes documents disagree. Example: Document A: 30-day retention Document B: 60-day retention Do not hide the conflict. Better answer: The sources provide different values. Document A states 30 days, while Document B states 60 days. Include citations for both. Confidence Through Retrieval Scores Retrieval systems often produce similarity scores. Example: Chunk A: 0.92 Chunk B: 0.87 Chunk C: 0.41 Low-scoring chunks may indicate weaker evidence. These scores can help: Filter poor matches Trigger fallback behavior Flag uncertainty Highlight Source Passages Many production systems show: Answer ↓ Supporting Passage Example: Answer: The warranty lasts 24 months. Evidence: "The warranty covers defects for 24 months..." Users can verify immediately. Citation Granularity Options: LevelExampleDocumentManual.pdfPagePage 42SectionAuthenticationParagraphParagraph 3ChunkChunk ID 17 Finer granularity usually improves trust. Grounding Metrics Evaluate: Citation Accuracy Does the cited source actually support the claim? Citation Coverage How many factual claims have citations? Hallucination Rate How often does the answer contain unsupported content? Answer Correctness Is the answer faithful to the retrieved evidence? Common Mistakes Citing Entire Documents Bad: Source: Handbook.pdf for a detailed claim. Too vague. Losing Metadata If page numbers disappear during ingestion: No precise citations possible. Allowing Unsupported Generation The model should not invent facts beyond retrieved evidence. Mixing Sources Without Attribution Users should know where each claim originated. Example Production Architecture Documents ↓ Chunking ↓ Embeddings ↓ Vector Store ↓ Retriever ↓ Chunks + Metadata ↓ LLM ↓ Answer + Citations Every retrieved chunk carries source information. Summary A grounded RAG application should: Store source metadata during ingestion. Retrieve text and metadata together. Prompt the LLM to answer only from retrieved evidence. Attach citations to individual claims whenever possible. Clearly indicate uncertainty when evidence is missing. Preserve page numbers, sections, URLs, and document identifiers. A good mental model is: Question ↓ Evidence Retrieval ↓ Answer Generation ↓ Source Attribution The strongest RAG systems do not merely generate answers—they generate answers that users can verify, with clear links back to the original evidence that supports each claim.

prompt: Explain how to keep a vector index up to date when the source documents change.
response: Keeping a vector index synchronized with changing source documents is a critical challenge in production RAG systems. A retrieval system is only as reliable as the freshness of its index. The core problem is: Documents Change ↓ Embeddings Become Stale ↓ Retrieval Quality Degrades A robust system needs mechanisms to detect changes, update embeddings efficiently, and maintain consistency between the source data and the vector database. The Naive Approach: Full Reindexing One simple solution is: Delete Index ↓ Reprocess Everything ↓ Rebuild Index Example: 10,000 PDFs Every night: Extract Chunk Embed Reindex Advantages Simple implementation Guaranteed consistency Disadvantages Expensive Slow Wasteful if only a few documents changed For small collections, this may be acceptable. For large collections, it quickly becomes impractical. Incremental Indexing Most production systems use incremental updates. Instead of: Reindex All Documents they do: Reindex Only Changed Documents Workflow: Detect Changes ↓ Process Changed Files ↓ Update Vector Store This dramatically reduces cost and latency. Assign Stable Document IDs Every document should have a unique identifier. Example: JSON{ "document_id": "employee_handbook_v1" } or: JSON{ "document_id": "contract_2025_001" } This ID is stored with every chunk. Example: JSON{ "chunk_id": "123", "document_id": "contract_2025_001" } Without stable IDs, updates become difficult. Track Document Versions Store version information. Example: JSON{ "document_id": "security_guide", "version": 7 } or: JSON{ "document_id": "security_guide", "last_modified": "2025-09-01T12:00:00" } When a newer version appears: Version 7 ↓ Version 8 the system knows an update is required. Detecting Changes Several methods are common. Timestamp-Based Detection Store: Last Modified Time Compare source and index values. Example: Source: 2025-09-01 Indexed: 2025-08-15 Document changed. Reindex it. Hash-Based Detection Compute a content hash. Example: Pythonimport hashlib hashlib.sha256(text.encode()).hexdigest() Store: JSON{ "hash": "abc123..." } If the hash changes: Old Hash ≠ New Hash the content changed. Hashing is often more reliable than timestamps. Document Lifecycle Events A source document can: Created Updated Deleted Renamed Moved Your indexing pipeline should handle all of them. New Documents Workflow: New Document ↓ Extract Chunk Embed Insert Simple append operation. Updated Documents Workflow: Updated Document ↓ Remove Old Chunks ↓ Generate New Chunks ↓ Insert New Embeddings This prevents stale content from remaining in the index. Deleted Documents Important but often overlooked. If: Document Removed then: Associated Chunks must also be removed. Otherwise retrieval may return content that no longer exists. Chunk-Level Updates Sometimes only a small portion changes. Example: Chapter 1 unchanged Chapter 2 unchanged Chapter 3 modified Chapter 4 unchanged Reembedding the whole document wastes resources. Instead: Reembed Only Changed Chunks This is known as partial reindexing. Chunk Hashing Store a hash per chunk. Example: JSON{ "chunk_id": "A17", "hash": "xyz123" } Compare: Old Chunk Hash New Chunk Hash Only changed chunks are reembedded. Example Original chunk: Access tokens expire after 60 minutes. Hash: A1 Updated chunk: Access tokens expire after 90 minutes. Hash: B2 Hash changed: A1 ≠ B2 Reembed only this chunk. Maintaining Metadata Each vector should include metadata. Example: JSON{ "chunk_id": "42", "document_id": "security_guide", "version": 8, "page": 42 } This makes updates and deletions straightforward. Soft Deletes vs Hard Deletes Hard Delete Remove vectors immediately. Delete Chunk ↓ Gone Soft Delete Mark as inactive. JSON{ "active": false } Retriever ignores inactive chunks. Useful when: Rollbacks are needed Auditing is required Event-Driven Indexing Modern systems often use events. Example: Document Uploaded ↓ Event Queue ↓ Indexer ↓ Vector Store Benefits: Near real-time updates Scales well Decouples ingestion from retrieval Technologies often used include message queues and streaming platforms. Scheduled Synchronization Another approach: Every 5 Minutes ↓ Check Sources ↓ Update Index Simple and reliable. Common for: Shared drives Wikis Document repositories Blue-Green Reindexing For very large collections: Current Index (Blue) New Index (Green) Build: Green Index in the background. After validation: Switch Traffic Advantages: No downtime Safe rollbacks Handling Embedding Model Changes Suppose you upgrade from: Embedding Model V1 to: Embedding Model V2 Vectors are no longer comparable. You typically need: Full Reembedding of all documents. Store: JSON{ "embedding_model": "text-embedding-v2" } to track compatibility. Consistency Challenges A common problem: Document Updated ↓ Vector Index Not Updated Users receive outdated answers. To avoid this: Monitor indexing lag Track update failures Validate synchronization Monitoring Freshness Useful metrics include: Index Lag Current Time - Last Indexed Time Failed Updates Failed Chunks Missing Documents Documents present in source but absent from index. Stale Documents Indexed version older than source version. Example Metadata Schema JSON{ "document_id": "security_guide", "chunk_id": "42", "page": 42, "hash": "abc123", "version": 8, "last_modified": "2025-09-01", "embedding_model": "v2" } This supports efficient updates and auditing. Typical Production Workflow Document Repository ↓ Change Detection ↓ Create / Update / Delete Events ↓ Chunking ↓ Embedding Generation ↓ Vector Database Update Retrieval always uses the latest indexed content. Recommended Strategy For most production RAG systems: Stable Document IDs + Content Hashes + Incremental Updates + Chunk-Level Reindexing + Metadata Tracking provides a good balance of simplicity, freshness, and cost. Summary To keep a vector index up to date: Assign stable document IDs. Track versions, timestamps, or content hashes. Detect document creations, updates, and deletions. Reindex only changed documents or chunks when possible. Store metadata with every vector. Remove or deactivate stale vectors. Monitor index freshness and failures. Rebuild the entire index when changing embedding models. Conceptually: Source Documents ↓ Change Detection ↓ Incremental Reindexing ↓ Updated Vector Store ↓ Fresh Retrieval Results The most scalable systems treat indexing as a continuous synchronization process rather than a one-time batch job, ensuring that retrieved answers always reflect the latest source content.

prompt: Explain how graph-based RAG works and when it beats plain vector retrieval.
response: Graph-based RAG augments retrieval with an explicit graph of relationships between entities, documents, concepts, sections, or facts. Instead of treating your knowledge base as an independent collection of chunks, it treats it as a connected network. This can dramatically improve retrieval for questions that require multi-hop reasoning, relationship discovery, or traversing connected information. Why Plain Vector Retrieval Has Limits Most RAG systems work like this: Documents ↓ Chunking ↓ Embeddings ↓ Vector Search When a user asks: How does OAuth2 token expiration affect API rate limiting? the system retrieves chunks that are semantically similar to the query. This works well when: The answer is contained in one chunk Relevant information is nearby Similar wording exists Example: Question ↓ Retrieve Chunk ↓ Answer However, many questions require combining information spread across multiple documents. Example: Which customers are affected by vulnerabilities in products supplied by Vendor X? The answer may require: Vendor X ↓ Product A ↓ Vulnerability CVE-123 ↓ Customer B No single chunk contains the complete answer. The Core Idea of Graph RAG Instead of storing only embeddings: Chunk A Chunk B Chunk C Graph RAG stores relationships: Chunk A ── related_to ── Chunk B │ mentions │ Entity X Knowledge becomes a graph. What Can Be Nodes? Common node types: Documents Sections Chunks Entities People Organizations Products Concepts Events Example: OAuth2 API Gateway Access Token Refresh Token Each becomes a node. What Can Be Edges? Edges represent relationships. Examples: uses depends_on belongs_to mentions causes located_in owned_by Example: OAuth2 └── uses ──> Access Token Access Token └── expires_after ──> 60 Minutes Building the Graph During ingestion: Document ↓ Chunk ↓ Entity Extraction ↓ Relationship Extraction ↓ Graph Construction Example text: OAuth2 uses access tokens. Access tokens expire after 60 minutes. Graph: OAuth2 │ uses │ Access Token │ expires_after │ 60 Minutes Retrieval in Graph RAG Traditional vector retrieval: Query ↓ Nearest Chunks Graph retrieval: Query ↓ Relevant Nodes ↓ Graph Traversal ↓ Connected Evidence Example query: How are refresh tokens related to access token expiration? Initial retrieval finds: Refresh Token Graph traversal then finds: Refresh Token ↓ renews ↓ Access Token ↓ expires_after ↓ 60 Minutes The answer emerges from connected nodes. Multi-Hop Reasoning This is where graph approaches shine. Consider: Which projects are impacted by a vulnerability in OpenSSL? Graph: OpenSSL ↓ used_by ↓ Service A ↓ part_of ↓ Project X The answer requires multiple hops. A vector search may retrieve: OpenSSL vulnerability but miss: Project X because they are not semantically similar. The graph explicitly connects them. Example: Company Knowledge Base Documents contain: Alice manages Team A. Team A owns Service X. Service X uses Database Y. Graph: Alice ↓ manages ↓ Team A ↓ owns ↓ Service X ↓ uses ↓ Database Y Question: Which database is used by Alice's team? Graph traversal naturally finds: Alice → Team A → Service X → Database Y Types of Graph RAG 1. Entity Graph RAG Nodes: People Companies Products Technologies Edges: works_for owns uses created_by Very common in enterprise systems. 2. Document Graph RAG Nodes: Documents Sections Chunks Edges: references cites related_to Useful for research corpora. 3. Knowledge Graph RAG Nodes: Structured facts Edges: Subject Predicate Object Example: Paris └─ capital_of ─► France 4. Hybrid Graph RAG Combines: Vector Search + Graph Traversal This is increasingly common in production systems. Hybrid Retrieval Workflow User Query ↓ Vector Search ↓ Seed Nodes ↓ Graph Expansion ↓ Evidence Collection ↓ LLM Example: Question: How does OAuth2 affect API security? Vector search finds: OAuth2 Graph expansion discovers: Access Tokens Refresh Tokens Scopes Authentication Server More complete context is retrieved. Why Graph RAG Beats Plain Vector Retrieval 1. Relationship Questions Question: How are A and B connected? Graphs are designed for this. 2. Multi-Hop Queries Question: Which customers use products containing vulnerable libraries? Requires traversing several relationships. 3. Sparse Mentions Two entities may never appear in the same chunk. Example: Document 1: Alice owns Service X Document 2: Service X uses Redis Graph traversal links them. 4. Better Context Expansion Vector retrieval often stops at: Top-K chunks Graph retrieval expands naturally through relationships. When Vector Retrieval Is Better Graph RAG is not always superior. Question: What is OAuth2? A simple semantic lookup works well. Graph traversal may add unnecessary complexity. Vector retrieval is often better for: FAQs Definitions Short factual questions Single-document lookups Storage Comparison Vector RAG Stores: Chunk ↓ Embedding Simple. Graph RAG Stores: Nodes Edges Embeddings Metadata More complex. Typical Graph Construction Pipeline Documents ↓ Chunking ↓ NER (Entity Extraction) ↓ Relationship Extraction ↓ Graph Database Common graph databases include: Neo4j TigerGraph Amazon Neptune ArangoDB Graph Traversal Example Suppose: A → B → C → D Query: Find information related to A. Graph retrieval can expand: A ↓ B ↓ C within a configurable hop limit. Common Retrieval Strategy Many systems use: 1. Vector Search 2. Find Seed Nodes 3. Traverse Graph 4. Collect Evidence 5. Rerank 6. Send to LLM This combines semantic understanding with explicit relationships. Challenges Graph Construction Extracting high-quality relationships is difficult. Bad extraction produces: Incorrect edges which lead to poor retrieval. Graph Growth Large enterprises may have: Millions of nodes Tens of millions of edges requiring careful scaling. Maintenance When documents change: Embeddings Graph Metadata must all remain synchronized. Practical Example Imagine an IT knowledge base: Employee Team Service Database Library Vulnerability Question: Which teams are affected by CVE-2026-1234? Graph path: CVE-2026-1234 ↓ Library X ↓ Service Y ↓ Owned By ↓ Team Z A graph can answer this naturally. A pure vector search may struggle because the relevant facts are distributed across multiple documents. Summary Plain vector RAG retrieves based on semantic similarity: Query ↓ Nearest Chunks It excels at: Definitions FAQs Semantic search Single-hop questions Graph-based RAG adds explicit relationships: Nodes + Edges and retrieves by: Query ↓ Seed Nodes ↓ Graph Traversal ↓ Connected Evidence Graph RAG typically outperforms plain vector retrieval when questions require: Multi-hop reasoning Relationship discovery Dependency analysis Entity-centric exploration Knowledge spread across multiple documents In practice, many advanced systems use hybrid retrieval—vector search to find relevant starting points and graph traversal to expand them—because it combines the strengths of both approaches.

prompt: Explain how to detect when a RAG system should say that it does not know.
response: One of the most important capabilities of a production RAG system is knowing when not to answer. A RAG system that confidently invents information is often worse than one that says: "I couldn't find enough evidence in the retrieved documents to answer that question." The goal is not merely to maximize answer rate—it is to maximize correctly grounded answers. The Core Problem A typical RAG pipeline looks like: Question ↓ Retriever ↓ Retrieved Chunks ↓ LLM ↓ Answer The problem is that LLMs are trained to produce plausible text. If retrieval fails: Question ↓ Poor Retrieval ↓ Little Evidence ↓ LLM ↓ Guess the model may still generate an answer. This is sometimes called a retrieval hallucination. What "I Don't Know" Actually Means A system should abstain when: Available Evidence < Required Evidence Examples: No relevant documents found Retrieved documents are only weakly related Sources conflict substantially Evidence is incomplete The answer requires information not present in the corpus Method 1: Retrieval Score Thresholds Most retrievers return similarity scores. Example: Chunk A: 0.91 Chunk B: 0.88 Chunk C: 0.84 Strong evidence. Example: Chunk A: 0.32 Chunk B: 0.29 Chunk C: 0.26 Weak evidence. Rule: If top score < threshold → Don't know Example: Pythonif top_score < 0.7: return "I couldn't find relevant information." Benefits Simple. Easy to implement. Limitations Similarity scores are not calibrated. A score of: 0.75 may be excellent in one corpus and poor in another. Method 2: Evidence Coverage Checks Ask: Does retrieved content actually contain the information needed? Example: Question: What is the refund period? Retrieved text: The company offers customer support. High semantic similarity may exist, but the answer is missing. Coverage test: Question Concepts ↓ Retrieved Concepts If key concepts are absent: No Answer Method 3: Retrieval Consensus Retrieve multiple chunks. Example: Chunk 1: Warranty = 24 months Chunk 2: Warranty = 24 months Chunk 3: Warranty = 24 months Strong agreement. Compare: Chunk 1: 24 months Chunk 2: 12 months Chunk 3: 18 months High disagreement. The system should either: Explain the conflict Refuse to provide a definitive answer Method 4: Grounded Generation Verification Generate an answer. Then verify whether every claim appears in retrieved sources. Pipeline: Question ↓ Retrieve ↓ Generate ↓ Verify Claims Example answer: Warranty lasts 24 months. Verification: Does retrieved evidence support: "24 months"? If not: Reject Answer Method 5: Citation Coverage Good RAG systems can attach citations to claims. Example: Claim A → Source Claim B → Source Claim C → Source Bad answer: Claim A → Source Claim B → Source Claim C → No Source Unsupported claims indicate hallucination risk. Rule: Unsupported Claim Ratio above threshold: Don't Know Method 6: Ask the Model to Judge Sufficiency Provide retrieved evidence and ask: Can this question be answered using only the provided context? Output: JSON{ "answerable": true, "reason": "..." } or: JSON{ "answerable": false, "reason": "Information missing." } This is often called an answerability classifier. Method 7: Train a Dedicated Classifier Production systems frequently use a model specifically trained to predict: Answerable vs Not Answerable Inputs: Question + Retrieved Chunks Output: Probability Answerable Example: 0.96 → Answer 0.22 → Abstain Method 8: Query Intent Detection Some questions inherently cannot be answered from a document corpus. Example: Who will win next year's election? or: What will our sales be in 2030? unless the corpus explicitly contains forecasts. The system should recognize: Question Type does not match: Knowledge Base Contents Method 9: Detect Out-of-Domain Questions Suppose the corpus contains: HR Policies Benefits Payroll Question: How does Kubernetes scheduling work? Retrieval may return weak matches. Domain mismatch suggests abstention. Pipeline: Question ↓ Domain Classifier ↓ In Domain? If not: Don't Know Method 10: Retrieval Margin Analysis Compare the best result to the next-best results. Example: Top Result: 0.91 Second: 0.52 Strong signal. Example: Top Result: 0.48 Second: 0.47 Third: 0.46 Ambiguous retrieval. Low margin can indicate uncertainty. Self-Consistency Checks Generate multiple answers independently. Example: Answer 1: 24 months Answer 2: 24 months Answer 3: 24 months High confidence. Compare: 12 months 24 months 18 months Inconsistency suggests uncertainty. The Gold Standard: Evidence-Based Answering The best approach is: Answer only if evidence exists. Prompt: Use only the provided context. If the answer cannot be determined from the context, say: "I couldn't find enough information in the retrieved documents." This dramatically reduces hallucinations. Example Workflow User Question ↓ Retriever ↓ Top Chunks ↓ Answerability Check ↓ Grounded Generation ↓ Citation Verification ↓ Final Answer Practical Confidence Signals A production system often combines several signals: SignalMeaningRetrieval scoreRelevanceScore marginAmbiguityCoverageInformation completenessCitation supportGrounding qualityConsensusAgreement across sourcesDomain matchCorpus relevanceAnswerability modelLearned confidence Confidence Fusion Example: Retrieval Score: High Coverage: High Citation Support: High Agreement: High Answer confidently. Example: Retrieval Score: Low Coverage: Low Citation Support: Weak Abstain. Common Mistakes Always Answering Many systems never say: I don't know. This maximizes hallucinations. Using Only Retrieval Scores High similarity does not guarantee the answer exists. Ignoring Source Conflicts Conflicting evidence should be surfaced. Allowing Unsupported Claims Every factual statement should be traceable to evidence. Example Responses Good: I couldn't find information about the warranty period in the retrieved documents. Better: I couldn't find information about the warranty period in the retrieved documents. The retrieved sources discuss customer support and returns but do not specify a warranty duration. Summary A RAG system should say "I don't know" whenever the available evidence is insufficient to support a grounded answer. The strongest production systems combine multiple signals: Retrieval Quality + Evidence Coverage + Answerability Detection + Citation Verification + Conflict Detection A useful mental model is: Can the answer be supported by retrieved evidence? If the answer is yes, generate a cited, grounded response. If the answer is no, the safest and most trustworthy behavior is: "I couldn't find enough information in the retrieved documents to answer that." This approach usually improves user trust and reduces hallucinations far more effectively than trying to force an answer for every question.

prompt: Explain how to build a semantic search engine for a collection of support tickets.
response: A semantic search engine for support tickets allows users to find relevant past issues even when they use different wording than the original ticket. For example: Query: "Can't sign in after changing password" should find tickets such as: "Users unable to authenticate after credential reset" even though the keywords differ. This is a classic use case for embeddings and vector search. System Architecture A typical semantic search pipeline looks like: Support Tickets ↓ Preprocessing ↓ Embedding Model ↓ Vector Index ↓ User Query ↓ Query Embedding ↓ Vector Search ↓ Ranked Results Step 1: Define the Ticket Structure Suppose tickets look like: JSON{ "ticket_id": "12345", "title": "Login fails after password reset", "description": "User reset password and now receives authentication errors.", "category": "Authentication", "status": "Resolved" } You typically search across: Title Description Resolution notes (if available) Step 2: Prepare Searchable Text Combine relevant fields into a single document. Example: Pythonticket_text = f""" Title: {title} Description: {description} Category: {category} """ Result: Title: Login fails after password reset Description: User reset password and now receives authentication errors. Category: Authentication This gives the embedding model richer context. Step 3: Clean the Data Typical preprocessing: Remove duplicate tickets Normalize whitespace Strip boilerplate signatures Remove system-generated noise Example: Before: Please do not reply to this email. Issue: Login fails... After: Login fails... Avoid aggressive text cleaning; modern embedding models generally handle punctuation and casing well. Step 4: Generate Embeddings Use an embedding model to convert tickets into vectors. Example workflow: Ticket Text ↓ Embedding Model ↓ Vector Example vector: [0.12, -0.44, 0.89, ...] Store one embedding per ticket or per ticket chunk. Step 5: Store Embeddings in a Vector Index For each ticket store: JSON{ "ticket_id": "12345", "embedding": [...], "title": "...", "status": "Resolved", "category": "Authentication" } Metadata is important because you'll often filter results. Step 6: Query Processing User enters: Unable to sign in after changing credentials Generate a query embedding: Query ↓ Embedding Model ↓ Query Vector Step 7: Vector Similarity Search Find the nearest ticket embeddings. Common similarity measures: Cosine similarity Dot product Euclidean distance Example results: TicketSimilarityLogin fails after password reset0.94Authentication timeout issue0.81MFA enrollment problem0.67 Simple Python Example Using NumPy: Pythonimport numpy as np def cosine_similarity(a, b): return np.dot(a, b) / ( np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b) ) scores = [ cosine_similarity(query_vec, ticket_vec) for ticket_vec in ticket_vectors ] top_indices = np.argsort(scores)[::-1][:10] In production, use an ANN index rather than comparing every vector. Step 8: Add Metadata Filtering Users often want constraints. Examples: Authentication issues only or: Resolved tickets from last year Apply filters before or during retrieval. Example: Pythonresults = search( query, category="Authentication", status="Resolved" ) Why Semantic Search Beats Keyword Search Keyword search: password reset may not match: credential recovery Semantic search understands that: password ≈ credential reset ≈ recovery and can retrieve relevant tickets. Hybrid Search (Recommended) Pure semantic retrieval sometimes misses exact identifiers. Example query: ERR_1042 Keyword matching is often better. A common production setup combines: BM25 + Vector Search Workflow: Query ↓ Keyword Search ↓ Vector Search ↓ Score Fusion ↓ Results This usually outperforms either method alone. Handling Long Tickets Some tickets contain: 10+ pages of logs and discussion. Instead of embedding the entire ticket: One Huge Ticket ↓ One Embedding split into chunks. Example: Issue Description Investigation Resolution Embed each chunk separately. Parent-Ticket Retrieval A useful strategy: Ticket ↓ Chunks Embed chunks for retrieval. When a chunk matches: Matched Chunk ↓ Return Full Ticket This improves precision while preserving context. Ticket Deduplication Support systems often contain duplicate issues. Example: User cannot log in Unable to sign in Login broken Semantic search can help identify near-duplicates. Process: New Ticket ↓ Embedding ↓ Similarity Search ↓ Potential Duplicates If similarity exceeds a threshold, suggest existing tickets. Using Resolution Notes Resolved tickets are especially valuable. Example: Issue: Login failure Resolution: Clear stale OAuth tokens. Include both issue and resolution in the indexed text. Then users can search: OAuth token problems and find the fix. Reranking Vector search may return 50 candidates. Use a reranker to improve ordering. Pipeline: Query ↓ Vector Search ↓ Top 50 ↓ Reranker ↓ Top 10 Rerankers examine query-document pairs more carefully and usually improve precision. Suggested Metadata Store fields such as: JSON{ "ticket_id": "...", "category": "...", "priority": "...", "status": "...", "created_date": "...", "resolved_date": "...", "assignee": "..." } These support filtering and analytics. Measuring Search Quality Create a test set: Query ↓ Expected Relevant Tickets Example: Query: Password reset login issue Expected: Ticket 123 Ticket 456 Evaluate with: Precision@k Recall@k MRR (Mean Reciprocal Rank) NDCG Example Production Pipeline Support Tickets ↓ Cleaning ↓ Chunking ↓ Embeddings ↓ Vector Database Search: User Query ↓ Embedding ↓ ANN Search ↓ Metadata Filters ↓ Reranking ↓ Results Scaling Considerations For small collections: 1,000–10,000 tickets simple vector search may suffice. For larger collections: 100,000+ use ANN indexes such as: HNSW IVF IVF-PQ to keep latency low. Enhancing with RAG Instead of returning only tickets: Query ↓ Search ↓ Relevant Tickets ↓ LLM ↓ Answer Example: User: Why am I getting authentication failures? System: Based on 14 similar resolved tickets, the most common cause is stale OAuth tokens after password changes. The retrieved tickets provide grounding for the answer. Recommended Production Design For most support-ticket systems: Support Tickets ↓ Clean & Normalize ↓ Chunk (if large) ↓ Embeddings ↓ Vector Index ↓ Hybrid Retrieval (BM25 + Vector) ↓ Reranker ↓ Results / RAG This design typically provides: Good semantic matching Strong exact-match performance Fast retrieval Scalability to large ticket collections Easy integration with LLM-powered support assistants The most effective systems usually combine semantic retrieval, keyword retrieval, metadata filtering, and reranking, rather than relying on embeddings alone.

prompt: Explain how to use Elasticsearch or OpenSearch for full-text and vector search.
response: Both Elasticsearch and OpenSearch can serve as a unified search platform that supports: Full-text search (BM25) Vector search (embeddings) Hybrid search (keyword + semantic) Filtering and aggregations RAG retrieval backends This makes them popular choices for production AI search systems because you can store documents, metadata, and vectors in one place. Search Paradigms Full-Text Search Traditional search: Query: password reset Document: Password reset instructions Matches based on terms and BM25 scoring. Vector Search Semantic search: Query: can't sign in after changing credentials Document: authentication failure after password reset Matches based on embedding similarity. Hybrid Search Combines both: Keyword Score + Vector Score Often gives the best results. Architecture Typical setup: Documents ↓ Ingestion ↓ Text Fields Metadata Embeddings ↓ Elasticsearch/OpenSearch Query path: User Query ↓ Embedding Model ↓ Vector Search ↓ Results Document Structure A support ticket might look like: JSON{ "ticket_id": "123", "title": "Login fails after password reset", "body": "User receives authentication errors...", "category": "Authentication", "embedding": [0.12, -0.44, 0.89] } The text fields support BM25. The embedding field supports semantic search. Creating an Index A typical mapping includes text, metadata, and vectors. Example: JSONPUT tickets { "mappings": { "properties": { "title": { "type": "text" }, "body": { "type": "text" }, "category": { "type": "keyword" }, "embedding": { "type": "dense_vector", "dims": 768 } } } } Text Field Types text Analyzed for full-text search. Example: JSON"title": { "type": "text" } Searchable with BM25. keyword Stored exactly. Example: JSON"category": { "type": "keyword" } Useful for: Filters Aggregations Exact matching Indexing Documents Example: JSONPOST tickets/_doc { "ticket_id": "123", "title": "Login fails after password reset", "body": "Authentication error after reset.", "category": "Authentication", "embedding": [...] } Documents become searchable immediately after indexing. Full-Text Search Simple BM25 query: JSONGET tickets/_search { "query": { "match": { "body": "password reset" } } } Elasticsearch/OpenSearch: Tokenizes text Computes BM25 scores Returns ranked results Multi-Field Search Search title and body together: JSONGET tickets/_search { "query": { "multi_match": { "query": "password reset", "fields": [ "title", "body" ] } } } Filters Example: JSONGET tickets/_search { "query": { "bool": { "must": { "match": { "body": "password reset" } }, "filter": { "term": { "category": "Authentication" } } } } } Filters do not affect ranking and are very efficient. Generating Embeddings Before vector search: Document ↓ Embedding Model ↓ Vector Example: Pythonembedding = model.encode(text) Store the vector in the index. Vector Search Basics User query: Can't sign in after changing credentials Generate query embedding: Pythonquery_vector = model.encode(query) Then search nearest vectors. k-Nearest Neighbor (kNN) Search Example: JSONGET tickets/_search { "knn": { "field": "embedding", "query_vector": [...], "k": 10, "num_candidates": 100 } } Workflow: Query Vector ↓ Nearest Neighbors ↓ Top Results Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search Large datasets require ANN indexes. Common structure: Vectors ↓ HNSW Graph ↓ Fast Search Both Elasticsearch and OpenSearch support HNSW. Benefits: Millisecond latency Scales to millions of vectors Hybrid Search Often the best approach. Combine: BM25 + Vector Similarity Example: JSON{ "query": { "bool": { "should": [ { "match": { "body": "password reset" } } ] } }, "knn": { "field": "embedding", "query_vector": [...], "k": 20 } } Why Hybrid Search Works Consider: ERR_1042 Keyword search excels. Consider: Unable to sign in after changing credentials Vector search excels. Hybrid systems benefit from both. Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) A common strategy: BM25 Results + Vector Results ↓ RRF ↓ Final Ranking RRF often improves retrieval quality significantly. RAG Retrieval Pipeline A common architecture: Documents ↓ Embeddings ↓ Elasticsearch/OpenSearch Query: Question ↓ Embedding ↓ Hybrid Search ↓ Top Chunks ↓ LLM Example: How long do access tokens last? Retrieved chunk: Access tokens expire after 60 minutes. Sent to the LLM for answer generation. Chunking for RAG Instead of indexing entire documents: 100-page manual split into: Chunk 1 Chunk 2 Chunk 3 ... Each chunk gets: Text Metadata Embedding This improves retrieval precision. Metadata Filtering Example: JSON{ "filter": { "term": { "document_type": "security" } } } Useful for: Department-specific search Permission filtering Date ranges Product filtering Security and Permissions Store access metadata: JSON{ "allowed_groups": [ "engineering", "security" ] } Then apply filters during retrieval. This prevents unauthorized documents from appearing in results. Updating Documents When a document changes: Document Updated ↓ Recompute Embedding ↓ Update Index Typical workflow: Detect Change ↓ Rechunk ↓ Reembed ↓ Update Documents Scaling Considerations Small Collections < 100k documents Simple deployments work well. Large Collections Millions of documents Use: Sharding Replication HNSW ANN indexes Dedicated ingest pipelines Monitoring Search Quality Measure: Precision@k How many returned results are relevant? Recall@k How many relevant documents are found? MRR How high do relevant results appear? NDCG Measures ranking quality. Common Production Architecture Support Tickets Knowledge Base PDF Chunks Wiki Pages ↓ Embedding Pipeline ↓ Elasticsearch/OpenSearch ↓ Hybrid Search ↓ Reranker (Optional) ↓ LLM Common Mistakes Indexing Entire Documents Large documents dilute embeddings. Prefer chunking. Using Only Vector Search Often misses: Error codes Product IDs Exact names Hybrid retrieval is usually stronger. Ignoring Metadata Filtering and security become difficult. Not Reembedding After Updates Results become stale. Oversized Chunks Very large chunks reduce retrieval precision. Example End-to-End Workflow Support Tickets ↓ Chunking ↓ Embeddings ↓ Index in Elasticsearch/OpenSearch ↓ User Query ↓ BM25 Search + Vector Search ↓ Hybrid Ranking ↓ Top Chunks ↓ LLM Answer Summary Elasticsearch and OpenSearch can act as a unified platform for: CapabilityPurposeBM25 SearchKeyword retrievalVector SearchSemantic retrievalHybrid SearchBest overall relevanceFiltersMetadata constraintsAggregationsAnalyticsSecurity FiltersAccess controlANN IndexesFast vector retrievalRAG BackendLLM grounding A common production pattern is: Chunk Documents ↓ Generate Embeddings ↓ Store Text + Metadata + Vectors ↓ Hybrid Search (BM25 + kNN) ↓ Optional Reranking ↓ Send Results to LLM This architecture provides strong exact-match retrieval, strong semantic retrieval, and a scalable foundation for enterprise search and RAG applications.

prompt: Explain entity linking and how it connects extracted mentions to a knowledge base.
response: Entity linking (sometimes called entity resolution, named entity disambiguation, or grounding) is the process of taking a mention in text and connecting it to the correct entity in a knowledge base. For example, if a document contains: Apple released a new product. the system must determine whether "Apple" refers to: Apple Inc. Apple Another entity with the same name Entity linking solves this ambiguity. The Entity Linking Pipeline Most systems follow four stages: Document ↓ Named Entity Recognition (NER) ↓ Mention Detection ↓ Candidate Generation ↓ Entity Disambiguation ↓ Knowledge Base Entity Step 1: Named Entity Recognition NER identifies spans of text that refer to entities. Example: Tim Cook spoke at Apple's annual event. NER might detect: Tim Cook Apple as entity mentions. Output: JSON[ { "text": "Tim Cook", "type": "PERSON" }, { "text": "Apple", "type": "ORG" } ] At this stage we know the mentions, but not which specific entities they refer to. Step 2: Candidate Generation For each mention, retrieve possible matching entities. Example: Apple Candidates: Apple Inc. Apple (fruit) Apple Records Apple Bank This step aims for high recall—it's okay to include extra candidates as long as the correct one is present. Sources for candidates include: Knowledge graph aliases Redirect pages Synonym tables Search indexes Wikipedia titles Step 3: Entity Disambiguation Choose the correct candidate based on context. Example: Apple released a new iPhone. Candidate scores: CandidateScoreApple Inc.HighApple (fruit)LowApple RecordsLow The surrounding words: released new iPhone strongly indicate Apple Inc. Why Entity Linking Is Needed Consider: Jordan won the championship. Possible meanings: Michael Jordan Jordan Someone whose surname is Jordan The mention alone is insufficient. Context provides the answer. Example of Context-Based Resolution Sentence: Jordan borders Saudi Arabia. Now candidates become: CandidateLikelihoodCountryHighAthleteVery low The neighboring words provide strong evidence. Knowledge Bases Used for Linking Common targets include: Wikidata DBpedia Enterprise knowledge graphs Product catalogs CRM databases Internal employee directories Knowledge Base Structure A knowledge base often stores: JSON{ "entity_id": "Q312", "name": "Apple Inc.", "aliases": [ "Apple", "Apple Computer" ], "type": "Company" } Each entity receives a unique identifier. Why IDs Matter Consider: Apple The string is ambiguous. The ID: Q312 is not. Once linked, all references point to the same canonical entity. Alias Matching Many entities have multiple names. Example: IBM and: International Business Machines refer to the same company. Knowledge bases store aliases: JSON{ "entity": "IBM", "aliases": [ "International Business Machines", "I.B.M." ] } Rule-Based Linking Simple systems use rules. Example: Pythonif mention == "iPhone": return "Apple Inc." Useful for: Small domains Product catalogs Internal business systems Not scalable to large knowledge bases. Search-Based Candidate Generation A common approach: Mention ↓ Search Index ↓ Top Candidates Example: Tesla returns: Tesla, Inc. Nikola Tesla Then a disambiguation model chooses the correct one. Embedding-Based Entity Linking Modern systems often use embeddings. Example: Context: Tesla announced vehicle deliveries. Create an embedding for: Tesla announced vehicle deliveries. and compare it against embeddings for candidate entities. The most semantically similar entity wins. Graph-Based Entity Linking Knowledge graphs can improve disambiguation. Example: Tim Cook Apple iPhone Graph: Tim Cook ↓ CEO of Apple ↓ makes iPhone The relationships reinforce each other. This is often called collective entity linking. Collective Disambiguation Instead of resolving each mention independently: Tim Cook Apple iPhone resolve them together. The system looks for a coherent set of entities. Example: Tim Cook → Apple Inc. Apple → Apple Inc. iPhone → Apple product These entities fit together logically. Confidence Scores Most systems produce: JSON{ "entity": "Apple Inc.", "confidence": 0.96 } Low-confidence matches may be: Flagged Sent for human review Left unresolved NIL Detection Sometimes no entity exists in the knowledge base. Example: AcmeAI Labs if the KB lacks that entity. Output: JSON{ "entity": null, "status": "NIL" } This is known as NIL detection. A good linker must know when not to link. Entity Linking in RAG Entity linking is useful during ingestion. Pipeline: Documents ↓ NER ↓ Entity Linking ↓ Knowledge Graph Example: Microsoft acquired GitHub. Stored as: Microsoft_ID ↓ acquired GitHub_ID This enables graph-based retrieval later. Entity Linking in Search Query: Issues related to Azure authentication Link: Azure ↓ Entity ID Search can then retrieve: Azure AD Azure Identity Azure documentation even if exact wording differs. Entity Linking in Analytics Suppose documents contain: IBM International Business Machines I.B.M. Linking maps all of them to the same entity. Analytics become accurate: Entity: IBM Mentions: 15,342 instead of fragmented counts. Common Challenges Ambiguous Names Example: Washington Could mean: State City Person Organization Short Mentions Example: AI Often insufficient context. Emerging Entities New companies may not exist in the KB. Domain-Specific Terminology Medical, legal, and scientific domains often require specialized knowledge bases. Enterprise Example Suppose a company knowledge graph contains: Employees Teams Services Databases Projects Document: Alice deployed Service X to PostgreSQL. Linked entities: Alice_ID Service_X_ID PostgreSQL_ID Graph: Alice ↓ deployed Service X ↓ uses PostgreSQL Now queries such as: Which services use PostgreSQL? can be answered directly from linked entities. Evaluation Metrics Common metrics include: Precision How many links are correct? Recall How many entity mentions were successfully linked? Accuracy Percentage of mentions linked to the correct entity. NIL Accuracy How often does the system correctly decide that no entity exists? Summary Entity linking transforms ambiguous text mentions into references to specific entities in a knowledge base. Example: Mention: Apple becomes: Apple ↓ Apple Inc. (Entity ID) The typical workflow is: Text ↓ Named Entity Recognition ↓ Candidate Generation ↓ Disambiguation ↓ Knowledge Base Entity Entity linking is valuable because it: Resolves ambiguity Connects documents to knowledge graphs Enables graph-based retrieval Improves search and analytics Supports multi-hop reasoning in RAG systems In modern retrieval and knowledge systems, entity linking is often the bridge between unstructured text and structured knowledge, allowing documents to participate in graph queries, relationship analysis, and more accurate semantic search.

prompt: Explain how to construct a test set of questions and gold answers for RAG evaluation.
response: A good RAG evaluation set is much more than a list of random questions. The goal is to create a benchmark that measures whether your retrieval and generation components work correctly under realistic conditions. A high-quality test set should answer questions like: Can the retriever find the right documents? Can the system combine information from multiple documents? Does it avoid hallucinations? Does it correctly say "I don't know" when the answer is absent? Does performance match real user behavior? Start with the Evaluation Goal Before writing questions, decide what you want to measure. Examples: GoalExample QuestionRetrieval qualityCan relevant chunks be found?Multi-hop reasoningCan information from multiple documents be combined?Grounded generationAre answers supported by sources?Hallucination resistanceDoes the system abstain when evidence is missing?Domain coverageDoes it work across all major topics? Different goals require different test sets. Define the Corpus Snapshot A test set must correspond to a specific version of the corpus. Example: Knowledge Base Version: 2026-09-01 If documents change later: Vacation Policy: 20 days becomes: Vacation Policy: 25 days your gold answers may become invalid. Always version the corpus used for evaluation. Collect Real Questions The best source is actual user behavior. Sources include: Search logs Support tickets Chat transcripts Help desk requests FAQ systems Product forums Example: User: How do I reset MFA if I lost my phone? Real questions are usually much better than invented ones. Create Question Categories A balanced evaluation set covers multiple retrieval scenarios. Example: CategoryExampleFact lookupWhat is the refund period?ProcedureHow do I reset my password?DefinitionWhat is OAuth2?ComparisonDifference between SSO and MFA?Multi-hopWhich teams own services using Redis?PolicyCan contractors access VPN?TroubleshootingWhy am I seeing error 1042? Without category coverage, scores can be misleading. Build Single-Hop Questions Single-hop questions require information from one source. Document: Access tokens expire after 60 minutes. Question: How long do access tokens last? Gold answer: 60 minutes. These evaluate basic retrieval quality. Build Multi-Hop Questions These require combining information. Documents: Service A uses Library X. Library X contains CVE-1234. Question: Which services are affected by CVE-1234? Gold answer: Service A. These test reasoning and retrieval depth. Include Paraphrased Questions Avoid copying document wording. Bad: Document: Vacation allowance is 25 days. Question: What is the vacation allowance? Better: How much paid time off do employees receive each year? This measures semantic retrieval instead of keyword matching. Include Negative Questions Some answers should not exist. Example: What is our Mars office address? if no Mars office exists. Gold answer: Not answerable from corpus. These are critical for measuring hallucination resistance. Create Gold Evidence Don't store only answers. Store supporting documents or chunks. Example: JSON{ "question": "How long do access tokens last?", "answer": "60 minutes", "evidence": [ "doc_12_chunk_4" ] } This allows retrieval evaluation independent of generation. Store Gold Chunks Example: JSON{ "question": "...", "gold_chunks": [ "chunk_41", "chunk_42" ] } Now you can compute: Recall@k Precision@k Hit rate without involving the LLM. Human-Written Gold Answers Gold answers should be concise and factual. Example: Question: Can contractors access VPN? Gold answer: Contractors may access VPN if approved by their manager and security team. Avoid overly verbose answers. Multiple Valid Answers Some questions have several acceptable phrasings. Example: JSON{ "answers": [ "60 minutes", "one hour" ] } Evaluation should account for semantic equivalence. Generate Synthetic Questions When real data is limited: Document ↓ LLM ↓ Question Generation Example prompt: Generate five realistic user questions that can be answered from this document. This can quickly create large datasets. Human Review Synthetic Data LLM-generated questions often have problems: Too easy Too similar to source text Ambiguous Artificial wording Review samples manually. Use Question Difficulty Levels Example: Easy What is the VPN timeout? Single document. Medium How can I reset MFA if my phone is lost? Several relevant passages. Hard Which customer-facing services depend on systems affected by CVE-1234? Multi-hop reasoning. Build an Evaluation Schema A common format: JSON{ "id": "q001", "question": "How long do access tokens last?", "answer": "60 minutes", "gold_documents": [ "security_doc_12" ], "gold_chunks": [ "chunk_45" ], "category": "fact_lookup", "difficulty": "easy" } This supports many evaluation metrics. Include Unanswerable Cases A production-quality benchmark usually includes: 10–30% unanswerable questions. Example: JSON{ "question": "What is our office in Tokyo's parking policy?", "answerable": false } These are essential for testing abstention behavior. Measure Retrieval Separately Retrieval evaluation: Question ↓ Retriever ↓ Retrieved Chunks Metrics: Recall@k Precision@k MRR NDCG Example: Gold Chunk: chunk_45 Retrieved: chunk_45 chunk_12 chunk_90 Recall@3 = 100%. Measure Answer Quality Separately Generation evaluation: Question ↓ Gold Context ↓ LLM ↓ Answer Metrics: Exact match F1 Semantic similarity LLM-as-judge Human review Evaluate Hallucinations Track: Unsupported claims Example: Question: How long do access tokens last? Evidence: 60 minutes Answer: 90 minutes Hallucination. Create Domain Coverage Targets Example: DomainQuestionsSecurity100HR100Infrastructure100Product100Legal100 This prevents overfitting to one area. Build a Multi-Hop Section Example graph: Team A ↓ Owns ↓ Service B ↓ Uses ↓ Library C Question: Which team uses Library C? These questions often reveal weaknesses hidden by simple fact-lookup benchmarks. Continuous Evaluation The test set should evolve. Workflow: Production Failures ↓ Analyze Root Cause ↓ Add New Test Case ↓ Prevent Regression Over time, your benchmark becomes increasingly representative of real-world usage. Example Mini Dataset JSON[ { "question": "How long do access tokens last?", "answer": "60 minutes", "gold_chunks": ["chunk_45"], "category": "fact_lookup" }, { "question": "Which services are affected by CVE-1234?", "answer": "Service A and Service B", "gold_chunks": [ "chunk_12", "chunk_88" ], "category": "multi_hop" }, { "question": "What is the Mars office address?", "answerable": false, "category": "unanswerable" } ] Recommended Composition For a production RAG benchmark, a common starting point is: 40% Single-hop factual questions 25% Procedural questions 15% Multi-hop questions 10% Comparative questions 10% Unanswerable questions Adjust these proportions based on your application's actual query distribution. Summary A strong RAG evaluation set consists of: A fixed corpus snapshot. Realistic user questions. Gold answers. Gold supporting documents/chunks. Answerable and unanswerable cases. Coverage across domains and difficulty levels. Separate evaluation of retrieval and generation. A useful mental model is: Question + Gold Evidence + Gold Answer + Metadata The most valuable benchmarks are usually built from real user questions, linked to authoritative evidence in the corpus, because they measure the behaviors that matter in production rather than synthetic success on idealized examples.
