prompt: I need to inspect staged changes when local and remote histories diverge. Give me the exact Git commands and explain each one.
response: When local and remote histories diverge, first understand the situation, then inspect the staging area. The important thing is: do not blindly git pull or reset before checking what you have locally. Example situation Suppose your branch is feature-login: C ── D ← local feature-login / A ── B \ E ← origin/feature-login C, D → commits you made locally E → commit that exists on the remote Both branches have different commits You also have some uncommitted/staged changes 1. Check your current branch Bashgit branch --show-current Expected: feature-login Make sure you're working on the intended branch. 2. Check the working tree and staging area Bashgit status Example: On branch feature-login Your branch and 'origin/feature-login' have diverged, and have 2 and 1 different commits each, respectively. Changes to be committed: modified: login.js Changes not staged for commit: modified: style.css This gives you two important pieces of information: Local/remote history → diverged Staged: login.js Unstaged: style.css 3. Inspect the staged changes Run: Bashgit diff --staged Example: Diffdiff --git a/login.js b/login.js --- a/login.js +++ b/login.js @@ - if (password.length < 4) { + if (password.length < 8) { This tells you exactly what is currently in the staging area. Remember: Bashgit diff → unstaged changes Bashgit diff --staged → staged changes 4. See which files are staged Bashgit diff --name-only --staged Expected: login.js If you see an unexpected file: login.js README.md config.js investigate before committing. 5. Fetch the latest remote history Before comparing local and remote commits, update your remote-tracking information: Bashgit fetch origin Important: git fetch downloads information about the remote but does not merge it into your working branch. Your working files remain unchanged. 6. Visualize the divergence Now run: Bashgit log --oneline --graph --decorate --all You might see: * d456abc (HEAD -> feature-login) Fix validation * c123abc Add login feature | * e789abc (origin/feature-login) Update login API |/ * b111aaa (main) This makes the divergence obvious: C ── D ← local / A ── B ───── \ E ← remote 7. Compare local-only commits Bashgit log --oneline origin/feature-login..feature-login This shows commits that exist locally but aren't on the remote. Example: d456abc Fix validation c123abc Add login feature 8. Compare remote-only commits Bashgit log --oneline feature-login..origin/feature-login Example: e789abc Update login API So now you know: LOCAL ONLY: C D REMOTE ONLY: E 9. Inspect the actual staged changes again The divergence doesn't change the meaning of: Bashgit diff --staged It still means: Show me changes currently staged for my next commit. For example: Local commits: C, D Remote commits: E Staged changes: login.js Unstaged changes: style.css These are separate concepts. 10. If you need to temporarily protect the staged changes If you need to rebase or otherwise reorganize your local commits, you may want to save your uncommitted work first. One option is: Bashgit stash push -m "WIP before resolving divergence" Then verify: Bashgit status After your history is synchronized, restore the work: Bashgit stash pop Then inspect again: Bashgit status git diff --staged If you specifically want to preserve staged state in the stash, use: Bashgit stash push --staged -m "Staged changes before sync" 11. Don't confuse staged changes with the divergence This is the key concept. Suppose your repository is: C ── D / \ A ── B ───────── ← local branch \ E ← remote branch And your working tree has: login.js → staged style.css → unstaged There are actually three different things to inspect: Commit history Bashgit log --oneline --graph --decorate --all Staged changes Bashgit diff --staged Unstaged changes Bashgit diff Don't assume that a divergence means your staged changes are part of either branch's commits. Staged changes are not commits yet. Safe diagnostic sequence When you discover that local and remote histories have diverged, use: Bashgit status Check branch + staged/unstaged state. Bashgit diff Check unstaged changes. Bashgit diff --staged Check staged changes. Bashgit fetch origin Update remote-tracking information. Bashgit log --oneline --graph --decorate --all Understand the history. Bashgit log --oneline origin/feature-login..feature-login See local-only commits. Bashgit log --oneline feature-login..origin/feature-login See remote-only commits. Then decide whether you want to merge, rebase, or otherwise reconcile the histories. One important rule Do not use git reset --hard just because the histories diverged. It can discard uncommitted working-tree changes. If your goal at this stage is simply to inspect what's staged, the safest core command is: Bashgit diff --staged and git status should be your first diagnostic command.

prompt: How do I inspect staged changes when local and remote histories diverge? Include a realistic example and the expected repository state afterward.
response: When local and remote histories diverge, you can inspect your staged changes without merging or rebasing first. The key is to separately inspect your staging area and the commit history. Step 3: Check exactly which files are staged Run: Bashgit diff --name-only --staged Expected: login.js If you accidentally staged style.css too, you would see: login.js style.css You could then unstage it: Bashgit restore --staged style.css The changes in style.css are not deleted; they simply move back to the unstaged area. Step 4: Inspect the divergence First update your knowledge of the remote: Bashgit fetch origin This does not merge anything into your branch. Then: Bashgit log --oneline --graph --decorate --all Example: * d456abc (HEAD -> feature-login) Fix validation * c123abc Add login feature | * e789abc (origin/feature-login) Update login API |/ * b111aaa (main) You can understand it as: C ── D ← local / A ── B ───────── \ E ← remote Step 5: Compare the local and remote commits Local-only commits: Bashgit log --oneline origin/feature-login..feature-login Example: d456abc Fix validation c123abc Add login feature Remote-only commits: Bashgit log --oneline feature-login..origin/feature-login Example: e789abc Update login API Now you know exactly how the histories differ. The main command for your actual question is: Bashgit diff --staged Think of it as: LOCAL/REMOTE HISTORY ↓ git log --graph │ │ STAGING AREA ↓ git diff --staged │ ↓ "What will my next commit contain?" So even when local and remote histories have diverged, git diff --staged still shows exactly what you have staged locally for the next commit.

Recovery Inspect it with: Bashgit diff --staged Remember: git diff ↓ unstaged changes git diff --staged ↓ staged changes 2. You accidentally staged an unrelated file Suppose you intended to stage: login.js but accidentally ran: Bashgit add . Now: Bashgit status shows: Changes to be committed: modified: login.js modified: style.css modified: README.md Diagnose Bashgit diff --name-only --staged Output: login.js style.css README.md Recovery Unstage the unwanted files: Bashgit restore --staged style.css README.md Then verify: Bashgit status Expected: Changes to be committed: modified: login.js Changes not staged for commit: modified: style.css modified: README.md Important: git restore --staged does not delete those changes. It only removes them from the staging area. 3. You think the remote branch has been updated, but it hasn't When histories diverge, your local information about the remote may be outdated. Diagnose Bashgit fetch origin Then: Bashgit status and: Bashgit log --oneline --graph --decorate --all Example: * D (HEAD -> feature-login) * C | * E (origin/feature-login) |/ * B This shows that local and remote have different commits. Recovery Don't immediately use: Bashgit reset --hard or blindly merge/rebase. First determine what is local-only: Bashgit log --oneline origin/feature-login..feature-login And what is remote-only: Bashgit log --oneline feature-login..origin/feature-login Now you know exactly what you're dealing with. 4. You accidentally unstage everything You might run: Bashgit restore --staged . Now your previously staged changes are unstaged. Diagnose Bashgit status You may see: Changes not staged for commit: modified: login.js Recovery Stage the intended file again: Bashgit add login.js Then: Bashgit diff --staged 5. Diagnose Bashgit diff --staged If you see unwanted changes, don't commit yet. response: If a secret was accidentally committed (API key, password, Firebase private key, .env file, etc.), the situation is different from merely staging a file. The most important rule is: Removing the secret from Git history does not make the secret safe. Rotate/revoke the secret first. Here's the beginner-friendly workflow. Example Suppose you accidentally committed: config.js containing: JavaScriptconst API_KEY = "abc123-secret"; Your commit history looks like: A ── B ── C ↑ secret 1. Inspect the latest commit Bashgit show --stat HEAD This shows which files were changed in the latest commit. If config.js appears, inspect it: Bashgit show HEAD -- config.js This shows the actual changes introduced by that commit. 2. Search your recent history for the secret/file For the filename: Bashgit log --all -- config.js For a specific string: Bashgit log -S'abc123-secret' --all --oneline -S searches commits where the number of occurrences of that exact string changed. You can also inspect a particular commit: Bashgit show <commit-hash> -- config.js 3. Immediately revoke/rotate the secret This is the most important recovery step. For example, if it is an API key: Old API key → REVOKE/DELETE New API key → CREATE Do this through the service that issued the credential. Why first? Even if you subsequently remove the secret from Git: Git history ↓ secret removed BUT Anyone who already obtained the old secret ↓ may still be able to use it Git history cleanup is not credential revocation. 4. Stop tracking the secret file If config.js should never have been committed, add it to .gitignore: Bashecho "config.js" >> .gitignore Then remove it from Git's index while keeping your local file: Bashgit rm --cached config.js Check: Bashgit status You should see something like: Changes to be committed: modified: .gitignore deleted: config.js The local config.js remains on your computer. 5. If the secret is only in the latest commit If the commit has not been pushed and you want to correct the most recent commit, you can reset it while keeping your work: Bashgit reset HEAD~1 Then remove the secret from the file and stage the safe version: Bashgit add config.js .gitignore Inspect before recommitting: Bashgit diff --cached Then: Bashgit commit -m "Remove secret from configuration" Your graph changes from: A ── B(secret) to: A ── B'(safe) B' is a replacement commit; the original B is no longer the branch tip. 6. If the secret was pushed to GitHub/GitLab Removing it from the latest file is not necessarily enough. For example: A ── B ── C ↑ secret Even if you make a new commit: A ── B(secret) ── C ── D(clean) the secret still exists in commit B. You need history rewriting to remove it from all relevant commits. For modern Git repositories, git filter-repo is generally preferred over the older git filter-branch. After rewriting history, you'll need to coordinate the rewritten history with collaborators and force-update the affected remote branches. Don't blindly run git push --force on a shared repository. For a repository hosted on GitHub or GitLab, also check the hosting service's secret-scanning/security guidance because cached copies, forks, pull requests, CI logs, or other systems may contain the exposed credential. 7. Final inspection Before pushing your cleaned history, check: Bashgit status Then inspect the current commit: Bashgit show HEAD Search history again: Bashgit log --all -S'abc123-secret' --oneline And search the working tree for the filename/content as appropriate. Also make sure .gitignore contains the secret file: Bashcat .gitignore 🚨 One important distinction If the secret was only staged: Bashgit restore --staged config.js is usually enough to remove it from the staging area. But if it was committed: Working directory ↓ Staging area ↓ Commit ↓ possibly Remote then simply unstaging it is too late. You need to consider: Rotate/revoke the secret Remove it from the current files Prevent it from being committed again with .gitignore/secret management If necessary, remove it from Git history If pushed, clean up the remote and other copies as appropriate Inspect the final history before continuing Never paste the actual secret into Git commands, chat, screenshots, or commit messages.

prompt: What can go wrong when I inspect staged changes when a merge produces conflicts? Show diagnostic commands and recovery steps.
response: When a merge produces conflicts, the main danger is thinking that git diff --cached shows the entire merge state. It only shows what is currently staged. Some files may still be conflicted. Here is a practical diagnostic and recovery workflow. 1. What can go wrong? Suppose you run: Bashgit merge feature-login and Git reports: CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in app.js Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result. Your repository can look like: MERGE IN PROGRESS │ ┌────────────┴────────────┐ ↓ ↓ README.md app.js STAGED CONFLICTED │ │ ↓ ↓ git diff --cached git diff So there are two different things to inspect. 2. Problem: git diff --cached appears empty You run: Bashgit diff --cached and see nothing. You might think: "The merge didn't produce any changes." Not necessarily. The conflict may simply be unresolved and unstaged. Check: Bashgit status You may see: Unmerged paths: both modified: app.js Then inspect: Bashgit diff You'll see something like: Diff<<<<<<< HEAD console.log("Welcome from main"); ======= console.log("Welcome from feature"); >>>>>>> feature-login Recovery Resolve the conflict in app.js, then: Bashgit add app.js Now: Bashgit diff --cached will show the resolved version. 3. Problem: You inspect only staged changes Suppose: Bashgit status shows: Changes to be committed: modified: README.md Unmerged paths: both modified: app.js If you only run: Bashgit diff --cached you see README.md, but you might forget about app.js. Recovery Always use: Bashgit status git diff --cached git diff Think: git status ↓ "What is happening?" git diff --cached ↓ "What is staged?" git diff ↓ "What is still unstaged/conflicted?" 4. Problem: You accidentally stage an unresolved/wrong resolution After editing app.js, you run: Bashgit add app.js Now Git considers the conflict resolved. But Git doesn't know whether your resolution is logically correct. So inspect it: Bashgit diff --cached Check that the final code is actually what you intended. For example, you wanted: JavaScriptconsole.log("Welcome from main"); console.log("Welcome from feature"); but accidentally kept only: JavaScriptconsole.log("Welcome from main"); Git won't necessarily tell you that your business logic is wrong. Recovery If you haven't committed yet, edit the file again: Bashnano app.js Then: Bashgit add app.js git diff --cached Repeat until the staged version is correct. 5. Problem: Conflict markers remain You may accidentally leave: <<<<<<< HEAD ======= >>>>>>> feature-login inside the file. Check with: Bashgit grep -n '<<<<<<<\|=======\|>>>>>>>' If anything is returned, inspect those files. Fix them, then: Bashgit add <file> and inspect again: Bashgit diff --cached 6. Problem: You use the wrong restore command Be careful with: Bashgit restore app.js This can discard unstaged changes in the working tree. If your intention is simply to remove a normally staged file from the staging area, use: Bashgit restore --staged app.js But with an unmerged file, be more deliberate: first inspect git status and the conflict stages before trying restoration commands. 7. Problem: You commit before checking everything You could run: Bashgit commit without carefully reviewing the resolution. Before committing, use: Bashgit status git diff --cached You want: All conflicts fixed but you are still merging. Changes to be committed: modified: app.js modified: README.md Then commit: Bashgit commit -m "Merge feature-login into main" 8. If you realize the merge was a mistake If the merge is still in progress and you want to abandon it: Bashgit merge --abort This attempts to return your working tree and index to the state they were in before the merge began. Then check: Bashgit status You should be back to the pre-merge state. Important Before aborting, make sure you understand what local work you have. Don't blindly use destructive commands such as: Bashgit reset --hard because that can discard working-tree changes. 9. If you already completed the merge Suppose: A ── B ───── M \ / C ─── ↑ merge commit and then you realize your conflict resolution was wrong. First inspect: Bashgit show --stat HEAD and: Bashgit show HEAD If the merge commit is already created, recovery depends on whether it has been pushed and whether other work has happened afterward. For a local, unpublished merge, you may be able to move the branch back carefully, but don't use reset --hard without first checking whether you have uncommitted work you need to preserve. 🔍 Diagnostic command cheat sheet ProblemCommandSee overall merge stategit statusSee staged changesgit diff --cachedSee unstaged changes/conflictsgit diffSee the merge commit afterwardgit show HEADFind conflict markersgit grep -n '<<<<<<<|=======|>>>>>>>'Stage resolved filegit add <file>Abort unfinished mergegit merge --abort 🧠 Safe workflow to memorize git merge feature ↓ CONFLICT ↓ git status ↓ ┌─────┴─────┐ ↓ ↓ staged conflict ↓ ↓ git diff git diff --cached ↓ edit/fix file ↓ git add file ↓ git diff --cached ↓ git status ↓ review everything ↓ git commit The golden rule Don't treat git diff --cached as a complete merge diagnostic. Use the combination: Bashgit status git diff --cached git diff Then, after resolving each conflict: Bashgit add <resolved-file> git diff --cached That gives you a clear view of what is conflicted, what is staged, and exactly what will enter the merge commit.

prompt: How do I inspect staged changes when a rebase stops at a conflict? Include a realistic example and the expected repository state afterward.
response: 👍 When a rebase stops at a conflict, the idea is very similar to a merge conflict, but there is one important difference: rebase is replaying commits one by one. Suppose you run: Bashgit rebase main and Git stops: CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in app.js error: could not apply abc1234... Add login feature Here is the exact workflow. 1. First check the rebase state Run: Bashgit status This is always your first command. You may see: interactive rebase in progress You are currently rebasing branch 'feature-login' on 'main'. You have unmerged paths: both modified: app.js It tells you: rebase is currently paused which commit Git is trying to replay which files have conflicts 2. Inspect the unstaged conflict Run: Bashgit diff You might see: Diff<<<<<<< HEAD console.log("Welcome to the exam portal"); ======= console.log("Login feature enabled"); >>>>>>> abc1234 Here: Bashgit diff means: "Show me the changes/conflicts that are currently in my working tree and have not been staged." 3. Inspect staged changes Now run: Bashgit diff --cached or equivalently: Bashgit diff --staged This shows: What is currently in the staging area and will be used when Git continues the rebase. It is possible for this to be empty even though git diff shows a conflict. That's completely normal. For example: Working Tree Staging Area ───────────── ───────────── app.js nothing │ └── conflict So: Bashgit diff shows the conflict, while: Bashgit diff --cached shows nothing. 4. Resolve the conflict Open app.js and change: JavaScript<<<<<<< HEAD console.log("Welcome to the exam portal"); ======= console.log("Login feature enabled"); >>>>>>> abc1234 to your intended final version, for example: JavaScriptconsole.log("Welcome to the exam portal"); console.log("Login feature enabled"); Remove all conflict markers. 5. Stage the resolved file Run: Bashgit add app.js This tells Git: "I have resolved the conflict in app.js." Now check: Bashgit status The file should no longer be listed under: Unmerged paths Instead, it should appear under something like: Changes to be committed: modified: app.js 6. Now inspect the staged resolution This is the part you're specifically asking about. Run: Bashgit diff --cached You should now see the resolved version that is staged. For example: Diff console.log("Welcome to the exam portal"); +console.log("Login feature enabled"); So the state has changed: BEFORE RESOLUTION Working Tree │ └── app.js = CONFLICT ↓ git diff AFTER RESOLUTION + git add Working Tree │ └── app.js = resolved ↓ git add app.js ↓ Staging Area │ └── app.js = resolved ↓ git diff --cached 7. Check for conflict markers Before continuing, you can check: Bashgit grep -n '<<<<<<<\|=======\|>>>>>>>' If it produces no output, those conflict markers aren't present in tracked files. You can also check whitespace/errors: Bashgit diff --check 8. Continue the rebase Once everything looks correct: Bashgit rebase --continue Git will continue replaying the commits. There are two possibilities. No more conflicts You may get: Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/feature-login. Done. Another conflict occurs Git stops again. Then repeat: Bashgit status git diff # resolve files git add <resolved-file> git diff --cached git rebase --continue A rebase can stop multiple times, because it replays commits individually. 9. What if the staged resolution is wrong? Suppose you ran: Bashgit add app.js but then notice: Bashgit diff --cached shows the wrong code. You can edit the file again: Bashnano app.js Then stage it again: Bashgit add app.js And inspect again: Bashgit diff --cached You don't need to restart the rebase. 10. What if you want to abandon the rebase? If you decide you don't want to continue: Bashgit rebase --abort This attempts to return your branch to the state it had before the rebase started. Then: Bashgit status to verify the repository state. Complete command sequence The workflow to memorize is: Bashgit rebase main If conflict occurs: Bashgit status git diff git diff --cached Resolve the file, then: Bashgit add app.js Inspect the staged resolution: Bashgit diff --cached Optional checks: Bashgit diff --check git grep -n '<<<<<<<\|=======\|>>>>>>>' Continue: Bashgit rebase --continue If another conflict appears, repeat the same process. 🔑 Merge vs Rebase The inspection commands are largely the same: MERGE CONFLICT git status ↓ git diff ↓ resolve ↓ git add ↓ git diff --cached ↓ git commit Whereas: REBASE CONFLICT git status ↓ git diff ↓ resolve ↓ git add ↓ git diff --cached ↓ git rebase --continue ↓ possibly another conflict ↓ repeat The biggest thing to remember is: During a rebase conflict, git diff --cached lets you inspect the resolved changes that are staged before you tell Git to continue replaying the current commit.

prompt: I need to inspect commit history after a teammate pushed new commits. Give me the exact Git commands and explain each one.
response: 👍 If your teammate has pushed new commits to the remote, the main goal is to update your knowledge of the remote history without accidentally changing your local work. Inspect the updated commit history Bashgit log --oneline --graph --decorate --all You might now see: * 8f42abc (origin/main) Add hall ticket download * 72bc991 Fix student authentication * d91a2f4 (HEAD -> main) Fix student login * 7c82b11 Add student seating page * 3fa91de Add Firebase authentication This tells you: HEAD -> main = your current local branch origin/main = latest remote branch 8f42abc and 72bc991 = commits your teammate pushed Your local main hasn't moved yet 4. See exactly which commits your teammate added Bashgit log --oneline HEAD..origin/main Example: 8f42abc Add hall ticket download 72bc991 Fix student authentication The meaning of: BashHEAD..origin/main is: Show commits that exist in origin/main but are not in my current HEAD. This is one of the most useful commands for this situation. 5. Inspect one of the new commits For example: Bashgit show 8f42abc This shows: commit message author date files changed actual code changes For a shorter summary: Bashgit show --stat 8f42abc Example: commit 8f42abc Author: Teammate Add hall ticket download student.html | 15 +++++++++++++++ app-v2.js | 8 ++++++++ 2 files changed 6. prompt: What can go wrong when I inspect commit history before opening a pull request? Show diagnostic commands and recovery steps.
response: Most commit-history inspection commands are safe/read-only, but problems usually happen when you accidentally run a command that changes the repository while trying to inspect it. Assume: feature/hall-ticket → main and you're preparing a PR. 1. You inspect the wrong branch You think you're on feature/hall-ticket, but you're actually on main. Diagnose Bashgit branch --show-current git status git log --oneline --decorate -5 Recovery If you have no uncommitted work: Bashgit switch feature/hall-ticket If you have uncommitted work, don't blindly switch. First inspect: Bashgit status git diff git diff --cached Your changes may need to be committed or stashed before switching. 2. You inspect an outdated main You run: Bashgit log --oneline origin/main..HEAD but haven't fetched recently. Your origin/main may be stale. Diagnose Bashgit fetch origin git log --oneline HEAD..origin/main Then inspect again: Bashgit log --oneline origin/main..HEAD Recovery Usually no recovery is needed. git fetch simply updates your remote-tracking information. 3. You accidentally use git pull You only wanted to inspect history, but you ran: Bashgit pull pull can fetch and then integrate changes into your branch. Diagnose Bashgit status git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all git reflog Look for a newly created merge commit or a changed HEAD. For example: Before: A ── B ── C ↑ HEAD After accidental pull: A ── B ── C ── M \ / D─E ↑ HEAD Recovery If an unwanted merge happened and you haven't made further work, first identify the previous HEAD: Bashgit reflog Example: abc1234 HEAD@{0}: pull: merge ... 91ab234 HEAD@{1}: checkout: moving ... Then, only after confirming there is nothing you need to preserve, you can return to the previous commit: Bashgit reset --hard 91ab234 ⚠️ --hard can discard uncommitted changes. Check git status first. 4. You accidentally run git reset --hard This is more dangerous. For example: Bashgit reset --hard origin/main could remove local committed/uncommitted work from your current branch. Diagnose Bashgit status git reflog Find your previous HEAD: 91ab234 HEAD@{1}: commit: Add hall ticket download Inspect it: Bashgit show 91ab234 Recovery Create a recovery branch first: Bashgit branch recovery-work 91ab234 Now your previous commit is safely referenced by: recovery-work ↓ 91ab234 Then you can decide how to restore your original branch. Important: reflog is good for recovering committed HEAD positions, but it cannot reliably recover arbitrary uncommitted changes destroyed by reset --hard. 5. You accidentally stage files Maybe you typed: Bashgit add . while preparing your PR. Diagnose Bashgit status git diff --cached --name-status You might discover: M student.html M app-v2.js A firebase-config.js and realize firebase-config.js shouldn't be staged. Recovery To unstage everything: Bashgit restore --staged . Or just one file: Bashgit restore --staged firebase-config.js This does not delete your working changes. 6. You confuse committed changes with uncommitted changes git log only shows committed history. Suppose: git log shows: 91ab234 Add hall ticket 72bc991 Fix seating display but you've also modified student.html. That modification won't appear in git log. Diagnose Use: Bashgit status git diff git diff --cached And to see all current changes relative to HEAD: Bashgit diff HEAD Mental model: Committed history ↑ git log Staged changes ↑ git diff --cached Unstaged changes ↑ git diff 7. You inspect the wrong PR range You might accidentally run: Bashgit log main..HEAD when your local main is outdated. Prefer: Bashgit fetch origin git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD And inspect the actual PR diff with: Bashgit diff origin/main...HEAD Diagnose which commits are on each side Bashgit log --oneline --left-right HEAD...origin/main Example: < 91ab234 Add hall ticket < 72bc991 Fix seating display > f55aa11 Fix Firebase configuration < = unique to your side. > = unique to origin/main. 8. You accidentally commit while preparing the PR Suppose you intended only to inspect but accidentally ran: Bashgit add . git commit -m "temporary" Diagnose Bashgit log --oneline -3 git status You might see: a12dd44 temporary 91ab234 Add hall ticket 72bc991 Fix seating display Recovery If the commit is local and hasn't been pushed, and you want to keep its changes staged: Bashgit reset --soft HEAD~1 Now: HEAD ↓ 91ab234 and the changes from a12dd44 remain staged. If the commit has already been pushed/shared, don't rewrite history without coordinating with the team. 9. You discover unrelated files in the PR Check: Bashgit diff --name-status origin/main...HEAD Example: M student.html M app-v2.js M README.md M personal-notes.txt If personal-notes.txt shouldn't be there, don't immediately reset everything. First determine whether it is: an uncommitted change, a staged change, or already committed. Bashgit status git log --oneline -- personal-notes.txt git diff origin/main...HEAD -- personal-notes.txt The recovery depends on which state it is in. 10. You accidentally switch branches with changes You might run: Bashgit switch main while having local changes. Git may refuse: error: Your local changes to the following files would be overwritten... Diagnose Bashgit status git diff If you need to temporarily save the changes: Bashgit stash push -m "work before PR inspection" Then switch: Bashgit switch main Later: Bashgit switch feature/hall-ticket git stash pop 🛡️ Safest diagnostic sequence If you're unsure what happened, don't start resetting things. prompt: What can go wrong when I inspect commit history after a pull request receives review comments? Show diagnostic commands and recovery steps.

Here are the common mistakes, with diagnostic commands and recovery steps. 1. You accidentally inspect the wrong branch You think you're on: feature/hall-ticket but you're actually on main. Diagnose Bashgit branch --show-current git status git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all Recovery If you have no uncommitted work: Bashgit switch feature/hall-ticket Then verify: Bashgit branch --show-current Expected: feature/hall-ticket 2. Your origin/main is outdated You run: Bashgit diff origin/main...HEAD but your local knowledge of origin/main is old. Diagnose Bashgit fetch origin git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all Then check: Bashgit log --oneline HEAD..origin/main If commits appear, main has commits your branch doesn't have. Recovery Usually, nothing needs to be "recovered." Just update your remote-tracking information: Bashgit fetch origin Then inspect again. 3. You accidentally use git pull You only wanted to inspect the remote history but ran: Bashgit pull Unlike git fetch, git pull also integrates the fetched changes. It could: fast-forward your branch create a merge commit start a rebase produce conflicts Diagnose Bashgit status git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all git reflog If you're in a merge/rebase, git status will tell you. For example: You are currently rebasing branch 'feature/hall-ticket' Recovery Don't immediately run random reset commands. First inspect: Bashgit reflog You may see: e82ab44 HEAD@{0}: pull: fast-forward 91ab234 HEAD@{1}: commit: Fix hall validation If you accidentally fast-forwarded and need to return to the previous commit, verify the old SHA first: Bashgit show 91ab234 Then, only if you're sure there is no work you need to preserve: Bashgit reset --hard 91ab234 ⚠️ --hard can discard uncommitted changes. 4. You accidentally run git reset --hard This is one of the dangerous mistakes. For example: Bashgit reset --hard origin/main Your local branch may suddenly move and local uncommitted changes can be lost. Diagnose Bashgit status git reflog Look for your previous HEAD: e82ab44 HEAD@{1}: commit: Fix hall validation Verify it: Bashgit show e82ab44 Recovery Create a recovery branch first: Bashgit branch recovery e82ab44 Now your previous commit is safely referenced: recovery ↓ e82ab44 You can then decide how to restore your feature branch. 5. You accidentally stage files You intended to inspect changes but accidentally ran: Bashgit add . Diagnose Bashgit status and: Bashgit diff --cached --name-status Example: M app-v2.js M firebase-config.js A secret.txt You notice secret.txt shouldn't be part of the PR. Recovery Unstage everything: Bashgit restore --staged . This does not delete your working changes. Then check: Bashgit status You should now see the files as modified but unstaged. 6. You confuse committed changes with uncommitted changes You run: Bashgit log and don't see your latest code changes. That's normal if you haven't committed them. Diagnose all three states Bashgit status git diff git diff --cached Think: Working Directory ↓ git diff ↓ Staging Area ↓ git diff --cached ↓ Repository / commits ↓ git log So: Bashgit log doesn't show ordinary uncommitted edits. 7. You inspect the wrong commit Suppose the reviewer commented on: d91a2f4 but you accidentally inspect: Bashgit show c45de12 Diagnose Verify the commit: Bashgit show --no-patch --oneline d91a2f4 Then inspect it: Bashgit show d91a2f4 No recovery is necessary because git show is only an inspection command. 8. Diagnose Bashgit log --oneline -3 git status If the commit is local and hasn't been pushed, and you want to remove the commit while keeping its changes staged: Bashgit reset --soft HEAD~1 Then: Bashgit status Your changes should still exist. ⚠️ If the commit was already pushed to the PR, don't rewrite shared history without considering the impact on collaborators. 9. You accidentally switch branches with uncommitted changes You have: app-v2.js modified and try: Bashgit switch main Git might refuse, or the changes might follow you if they don't conflict. You accidentally compare the wrong ranges These commands answer different questions. PR commits Bashgit log origin/main..HEAD Which commits are on my branch but not main? Review-fix changes Bashgit diff d91a2f4..e82ab44 What changed between the old and new commits? Complete PR changes Bashgit diff origin/main...HEAD What is the overall PR diff from the common base? Mixing these up can make you think a change is missing when it isn't. 🛟 Safest diagnostic sequence If you're confused after inspecting the PR, stop making changes and run: Bashgit status git branch --show-current git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all git diff git diff --cached git reflog git rev-parse HEAD This gives you: status → What state am I in? branch → Where am I? log → What is the history? diff → What is unstaged? diff --cached→ What is staged? reflog → Where has HEAD been? rev-parse → What commit am I currently on? ⭐ Golden rule For inspection, prefer: Bashgit status git log git show git diff git reflog git fetch Be careful with commands that change repository state: Bashgit pull git reset git restore git switch git add git commit git rebase Especially avoid using git reset --hard or git restore just to "see what happens." First inspect the state, identify the exact commit you need, and only then perform a recovery operation.

prompt: Explain inspect commit history when a secret was accidentally committed using a commit graph or file-state example where useful.
response: The easiest way to understand this is to separate committed history from the current file state. 1. Imagine the commit graph Suppose your project has: A ── B ── C ── D ↑ HEAD For your exam-seating project: A Initial project │ B Add Firebase authentication │ C Add student seating page │ D Add Firebase configuration ← secret accidentally committed D might be: d91a2f4 The important point is: The secret is now part of commit D. It isn't just a working-directory change. 2. Understand the file state Imagine the repository currently looks like this: COMMIT HISTORY │ ↓ D (HEAD) │ │ contains ↓ firebase-config.js ┌──────────────────┐ │ apiKey = "SECRET" │ └──────────────────┘ There may also be new local changes: HEAD = D Staging Area: app-v2.js Working Directory: student.html So there are three different things to inspect: HEAD / COMMITTED │ ↓ git show D STAGING AREA │ ↓ git diff --cached WORKING DIRECTORY │ ↓ git diff 3. Inspect the commit itself Start with: Bashgit show --stat d91a2f4 This answers: "Which files did this commit change?" Then: Bashgit show d91a2f4 -- firebase-config.js This answers: "What exactly did this commit change in firebase-config.js?" You might see: Diff+ const apiKey = "SECRET_VALUE"; So you've confirmed that the secret entered the repository in that commit. 4. Inspect the file's history Run: Bashgit log --all --oneline -- firebase-config.js Example: d91a2f4 Add Firebase configuration c45de12 Add Firebase authentication a12bc44 Initial project This answers: "Which commits changed this file?" To specifically search for the secret: Bashgit log -S"SECRET_VALUE" --all --oneline If you get: d91a2f4 Add Firebase configuration then that exact text was introduced/changed there. 5. Check whether the secret exists elsewhere This is important because deleting it from the current file doesn't automatically remove it from history. Bashgit grep -n "SECRET_VALUE" $(git rev-list --all) Conceptually: A ── B ── C ── D ── E ↑ secret here E may have: apiKey = "NEW_VALUE" But D still has: apiKey = "SECRET_VALUE" Git remembers old snapshots. 6. Check whether the bad commit was pushed First: Bashgit fetch origin Then: Bashgit branch -a --contains d91a2f4 You might see: * feature/firebase remotes/origin/feature/firebase That means the remote-tracking branch contains the bad commit. If the secret was pushed, treat the credential as exposed and revoke/rotate it. Removing it from the current version alone doesn't make the old credential safe. 7. What should the repository look like after inspection? If you only run inspection commands such as: Bashgit status git log git show git diff git fetch the commit graph should remain: A ── B ── C ── D ↑ HEAD And your local file state should remain unchanged: COMMITTED: D └── firebase-config.js contains the old secret STAGED: app-v2.js UNSTAGED: student.html Verify with: Bashgit status git rev-parse HEAD HEAD should still be: d91a2f4... 🧠 The key mental model git log ↓ "What commits exist?" git show <commit> ↓ "What did this commit contain?" git log -- <file> ↓ "Which commits changed this file?" git log -S"secret" --all ↓ "Where did this exact text appear/change?" git diff --cached ↓ "What is staged right now?" git diff ↓ "What is modified but unstaged?" So inspecting history doesn't fix the secret. It tells you where the secret entered Git, whether it exists elsewhere, and whether the bad commit reached a remote. After that, credential rotation and, if appropriate, history cleanup are separate steps.

prompt: I need to inspect commit history when a merge produces conflicts. Give me the exact Git commands and explain each one.
response:
When a merge produces conflicts, the safest approach is to inspect the history and conflict state before trying to resolve anything. Let's assume you're merging: Bashgit merge feature/hall-ticket into main, and Git reports conflicts. 1. Check the current repository state Bashgit status This is the first command to run. Example: On branch main You have unmerged paths. Unmerged paths: both modified: student.html both modified: app-v2.js It tells you: you're in the middle of a merge which files are conflicted whether anything else is staged or modified 2. Confirm the current branch Bashgit branch --show-current Expected: main This prevents accidentally inspecting the wrong branch. 3. Inspect the commit history Bashgit log --oneline --graph --decorate --all You may see: * 91ab234 (HEAD -> main) Fix Firebase configuration |\ | * 72bc991 (feature/hall-ticket) Add hall ticket download | * 63de221 Add hall ticket button * | 55aa11 Update student login |/ * 42bc100 Initial project The graph helps you understand where the two histories diverged. 4. Inspect the commits on the feature branch Bashgit log --oneline main..feature/hall-ticket This means: Show commits reachable from feature/hall-ticket that aren't in main. Example: 72bc991 Add hall ticket download 63de221 Add hall ticket button 5. Inspect commits that are only on main Bashgit log --oneline feature/hall-ticket..main Example: 91ab234 Fix Firebase configuration 55aa11 Update student login Now you know what each side contributed. 6. Inspect the conflicting files Start with: Bashgit status Then inspect a particular file: Bashgit diff -- student.html You'll see conflict markers such as: <<<<<<< HEAD

Student Seating

=======

Hall Ticket & Seating

>>>>>>> feature/hall-ticket Meaning: <<<<<<< HEAD ↓ Your current branch's version ======= ↓ Merged branch's version >>>>>>> feature/hall-ticket 7. See all unresolved conflicts Bashgit diff --name-only --diff-filter=U Example: student.html app-v2.js U means unmerged. 8. Inspect each side of a conflicted file For a conflicted file: Bashgit show :2:student.html This shows the ours/current branch version. Bashgit show :3:student.html This shows the theirs/merged branch version. So: :2 → ours → main :3 → theirs → feature/hall-ticket This is extremely useful when the conflict markers aren't enough. 9. Inspect the merge base You can find the common ancestor: Bashgit merge-base main feature/hall-ticket Suppose it returns: 42bc100 Then inspect it: Bashgit show --stat 42bc100 Or inspect a file at the common ancestor: Bashgit show 42bc100:student.html Now you can compare: 42bc100 / \ / \ main feature ↓ ↓ OURS THEIRS This helps explain why Git considers the changes conflicting. 10. Compare the branches You can inspect the overall difference: Bashgit diff main...feature/hall-ticket Or a summary: Bashgit diff --stat main...feature/hall-ticket Be careful with the meaning: git log main..feature ↓ commits only on feature git log feature..main ↓ commits only on main git diff main...feature ↓ changes from their common ancestor toward feature 11. Verify before resolving Before making any resolution changes: Bashgit status git rev-parse HEAD Record the HEAD SHA. You can also check: Bashgit diff --check This can identify whitespace errors in the current diff. Complete inspection sequence For a merge conflict, I'd use: Bashgit status git branch --show-current git rev-parse HEAD git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all git log --oneline main..feature/hall-ticket git log --oneline feature/hall-ticket..main git diff --name-only --diff-filter=U git diff -- student.html git diff -- app-v2.js git show :2:student.html git show :3:student.html git merge-base main feature/hall-ticket git diff --stat main...feature/hall-ticket git status git rev-parse HEAD Important These commands inspect the merge state. They don't resolve the conflict. After you've understood the differences, you can decide whether to edit the files, use git checkout --ours/--theirs or git restore --ours/--theirs, stage the resolved files, and complete the merge. Don't run git reset --hard just to "get a clean view"—it can discard local work.
